Clybourn, Jonas against S Clybourn: an initial S does not expand to Jonas, and the layer holds no other candidate.
Crafts, John — the layer holds no Crafts, and this is the trader whom bk_afc_010 and the old-settler notice put dead at Chicago in 1823 or 1825.
Galloway, James — a name, a state, a year and one civic act, and no Galloway in the residents layer.

Jouett, Charles — first Indian agent, the remarks cell reading 'left in 1881' where the digits are one transposition from 1811 and Jouett's agency ended that year. An office of 1805-11 and no card in the layer.
Kinzie, John — the row's own remarks cell ends 'died 1828', which is John Kinzie the ELDER. He belongs in no 1835 record at all and the crosswalk refuses him onto his son's card.
Kelly, Henry — the only occupation in the remarks column, and it describes 1828. The layer's nearest name is Wilham MKelly, a different man's card, and no merge is proposed.

Laframboise, Henry, Sr against Josette LaFramboise Beaubien, the only bearer of the surname in the layer and a woman already written into another household. The nativity cell prints the compiler's racial classification of 1895 where a birthplace belongs and is recorded as it stands.
Laframboise, Henry, Jr — refused on the same ground, and the row is a name and a ditto with no year and no remarks of its own.
Laframboise, Claude — refused on the same ground; the nativity cell is a ditto of the row above and resolves to the compiler's classification, not to a birthplace.
Laframboise, Joseph — refused on the same ground. The four Laframboise rows are refused one by one and not as a block.

Laughton, Barney H — nativity New England, year 1827, no remarks. The books crosswalk merges the row onto 'Barnardus H Laughton' on the middle initial and the everyday form of the forename, AND THAT CARD IS GONE: hh_laughton_barnardus_h.json was minted from a Chicago paper printing the name, and T-1049 (PR #1175) withdrew it when the resolved place vocabulary read the notice as naming a man outside the town. The layer's two Laughton cards today are David and Sophia, neither a Barney nor a B., and joining the table's row to either would be a surname merge, which this domain's standing rule makes a refusal. T-1322 read the row and declined to re-mint the withdrawn card from it.

Miller, Samuel — no nativity cell, a year of 1827 and one civic act, against a civic-mint card whose earliest bound is the muster of 1832. A common name with nothing beside it is exactly what this domain refuses on.
Ouilmette, Antoine — the layer holds no Ouilmette. On the nativity cell, see the Laframboise rows: it is the compiler's classification and not a birthplace.
Scott, Stephen against John Scott, the only Scott this layer holds; different forenames, both printed whole.

Scott, Willard (the scan doubling an i) against John Scott; different forenames, both printed whole. The row also contradicts itself as printed — an 1828 arrival and a vote in 1826 — and the contradiction is recorded rather than resolved.
Scott, Willis against John Scott; different forenames, both printed whole. The three Scott rows are refused one by one.
See, William — a one-syllable surname the layer holds no card for at all.
Wolcott, Alex — Dr Alexander Wolcott the Indian agent, who came to the agency in 1820 and died on 25 October 1830, refused onto the town's card of that name rather than merged.
Walker, Rev. Jessa — Rev. Jesse Walker, the Methodist itinerant of the Illinois circuit, against Jeremiah Walker, the nearest of the four Walkers this layer holds. Different forenames.

Welch, Michael — nativity Ire, year 1829, no remarks, against Michael P Welch, a civic-mint card with a middle initial and a bound of 24 December 1834. The crosswalk says what it would take to spend the row and this pass does not supply it.

Andreas on how Chicago got its water between the public well of November 1834 and the Hydraulic Company's works of 1842: two-wheeled carts with a mounted hogshead driven into the lake at the foot of Randolph, filled by pail and run off through a leathern hose into barrels at a customer's door at five to ten cents. T-0759 took it and is closed: data/yard/town_water_cart.json cites this claim by id, and data/liberties.json and docs/LIBERTIES.md carry what was inferred from it. The cart is yard furniture, not a household and not a firm — the reading's own notes say the trade was never minuted and name no waterman — so there is no record on either indexed layer for this unit to be asserted against. It routed to T-1468 as 'a trade the town ran that no business record carries'; T-1468's last live child closed on 2026-09-21 (T-1509) and the routing had nowhere left to point.

A store standing empty and advertised to let in June 1835. The notice gives no street and the advertiser's name survives only as the fragment 'dM KINZ' in the adjoining column, which the reading itself refused to make an entity. An empty store is a building; this one has no seat and is counted as stock.

Two dwellings and a third building whose kind is illegible ('idee'), offered together by C. H. Chapman. The 1835-06-20 printing of the same notice sets the third as a stable; neither printing names a street. Three buildings in one hand is a count the household layer can eventually use and a placement it cannot.

The same Chapman group as 1835-06-08, with the third building now legible as a stable: two dwellings and a stable offered together. A dwelling pair with a stable behind is a yard shape the household layer builds, and still no street is printed in either issue, so nothing chooses which yard it is.

A house on Lake Street, to let, in the week before the scene date. The corridor is named and that is as far as it reaches: Lake Street carries dozens of frontages in the address book and the notice gives no corner, no number and no neighbour, so no seat on it is more likely than any other. The forty acres of section 4 advertised beside it are county land and are not a building.

The Chicago Reading Room has a board of directors, a subscription costed at $2,500 to $3,000, and no premises: the board meets at the Tremont House on 6 July precisely to consult on means of obtaining a building. On the scene date there is no reading-room building, and this notice is the evidence that there is not.

The directors resolve that a joint-stock company might put a building for the Reading Room on the Public Square under a rent-free lease. A building that a committee believes a lease can PROBABLY be obtained for is not a building: on 1835-07-01 the square carries no reading room and nothing else this notice proposes.

A three-storey store rented whole as an auction room, advertised on 1 August 1835 — the only building in this corpus documented at more than one storey by its own count. Neither of the two street names printed with it is legible ('IWarpom' street, 'lo. Ly' street) and neither is guessed at, so the reading dates and describes and does not place.

Eight thousand bricks and a mason to lay them, wanted at B. Beaubien's store at the end of August 1835 — the only masonry evidence in eleven weeks of this paper, against oak scantling, seasoned lumber, five lumber cargoes and hand-made sash. It corroborates a plank town with brick as the exception and moves nothing standing on 1 July.

A store, a dwelling and a large house 'suitable for a Boarding House' in C. H. Chapman's hands, in the month the same paper reports every room in the public houses taken and strangers sleeping on floors. None of the four printings names a street for any of the three, so all three are building stock and none is a placement.

A house on Randolph Street 'nearly opposite the public square' — the best anchor any placeless notice in this run carries, because the square is a surveyed block the reconstruction already stands on. It is still not a seat: 'nearly opposite' spans the whole Randolph frontage of the block and the address book would have to pick one of them.

A store of 20 by 45 feet including its counting room, with three rooms let separately as offices, in Kinzie's Addition — the only MEASURED commercial building in this reading range, which is the reason the measurement is recorded here rather than lost. Kinzie's Addition is a whole addition north of the main branch and the notice names no lot in it, so the figure has no building to sit on yet.

John T. Temple lets two stores — one on South Water, one on Lake — and a dwelling. Both of the town's principal streets are named and neither store is: no corner, no number, no neighbour. What the notice establishes is lettable empty commercial floor on both streets in late May 1835, which is an aggregate and is recorded as one.

A store house — a warehouse — on Water Street, let by David Carver, the town's lumber dealer and commission merchant. The river street is named and the building is not placed on it. The trade attached to the man is a business reading and is not this unit.

A dwelling house 'lately erected by Mr. Rezigue' in Kinzie's Addition, to let and standing empty in June 1835. 'Lately erected' dates it to the months before the scene date and that is the fact; the addition is named and no lot in it is, and Rezigue is a single crop-edge reading that the extraction itself declined to make an entity.

The Eagle Coffee House, Trowbridge's, ruled. The house stands: the town's Democrats meet in it on Monday 29 June 1835, two days before the scene date, and the parenthetical '(TROWBRIDGE'S)' is how the town identified it. The street is DOCUMENTED, which is the part the hand-off could not reach — the Abell advertisement whose preposition the 24 June interleave destroyed is reprinted whole in the Democrat of 5 August 1835 over the same 24 June copy date, and reads 'in Dearborn stre[et], two doors south of the "Eagle Coffee House"' (1835_08_05#c020); the tailors Cooley and Hol[b]man put their shop 'on Dearborn Street, nearly opposite' it (1835_08_05#c005). The SEAT is not reachable, because both of those addresses are themselves unseated and measured from the Eagle rather than from the plat: the only fixed term in the set is Dearborn Street. So the reading closes in the aggregate as building stock on a named street, no structure is raised, and data/exclusions.json#eagle_coffee_house carries the guard. The business layer's biz_eagle_tavern and biz_eagle_hotel are still NOT this house — they are 1834 firms under other keepers, and identity.json says so in terms.

The corner stone of a NEW Baptist meeting house is to be laid on 4 July 1835, one block south of the public square. Three days after the scene date, so on 1 July there is no such building — only a site a block south of the square and a ceremony announced. The existing Baptist meeting house that District No. 2 meets in is a different building and is handed to T-1600 separately.

The left-hand ends of the same printed lines as c007, kept as their own claim because they are in another column and because 'One block' — the only thing in the issue that puts the new meeting house anywhere — is here. Same refusal, same reason: the corner stone is laid on 4 July and the building does not exist on the scene date.

The Rezigue dwelling again, and this printing's line ends 'erected by Mr. Rezigue, on' with the crop taking the street. The reading deliberately does not supply it. A large dwelling house lately built and standing empty is building stock; where it stood is not in this corpus.

The Reading Room's directors meet at the Tremont House on 13 July and resolve to seek about two thousand dollars of joint stock for a building containing the reading room and usable as a meeting or lecture room, on the understanding that a site could be had on the Public Square. A building proposed is not a building standing, and nothing in the 1835 model may stand on it.

'A good Store to let — Apply to JOHN T. TEMPLE', 29 July 1835. An empty store is a building and this one is four weeks after the scene date with no street given, so it neither places anything nor reaches 1 July. Temple is documented elsewhere in the town and the notice places neither him nor the store.

'The New Store on Dearborn st.', rented for an auction and commission business in August 1835, with no owner, no number and no neighbour — the definite article doing all the work, which is itself the finding about how small the town was. The printing is unsigned, so the claim is a building and not a business, and it is six weeks later than the scene.

Two stores standing empty and advertised to let, dated 20 July and printed 12 August 1835 — the only vacancy the month advertises, and it says nothing about where they are. The surname is set 'SEMPLE' here and 'TEMPLE' on 19 August; neither printing is merged into the other, because identity.json is the only place that judgement may be made.

The same two empty stores, and this printing sets the name as TEMPLE against the 12 August column's 'SEMPLE'. Still no address in either printing, and still after the scene date: it corroborates the 12 August reading and adds no 1 July fact.

The Green Tree Hotel named, with a waggon standing beside it overnight on 7 or 8 August 1835 carrying two hundred dollars in coin, and robbed. The use is vivid and it is dated five weeks after the scene; it corroborates the house the structure layer already holds and moves nothing on 1 July.

A second named Chicago inn used as an address: information about a strayed bay horse to be left 'at the New [York] House'. The supplied word is bracketed and is the least certain reading in the claim. August 1835, so it corroborates and does not place.

Chester Ingersoll's house is the Chicago Magistrates District's polling place for the constable election of 9 December 1833 — a house public enough to hold an election, named by its keeper. The notice gives no street and no anchor of any kind, and the committed town holds no Ingersoll house for it to be, so nothing can receive it.

John Wright's 'Two Buildings to Let' of 26 November 1833 is the notice the town's `wright_building_to_let_a` and `wright_building_to_let_b` stand on: both records cite `chicago_democrat_1833_11_26` and both `documented_range` notes quote this advertisement and reason from its 1 June 1834 term. The reading raised two roofs in the committed town and the ledger cannot see them because they are structures and not people.

The corporation's fire ordinance of 26 November 1833, clause 6: a stove pipe passed through a wooden or lath-and-plaster partition, guarded by earthenware, brick, tin or sheet iron, standing at least eighteen inches proud of the roof. That is a specification for the whole town's roofline — stove pipes and not masonry stacks — and it attaches to no one roof, so it is spent on the town.

Lot 7 in block 8, with the house on it 'formerly occupied as a Meeting House', cried at the Eagle Hotel on 13 December 1833. BLOCK 8 IS READ: Wright's numeral puts it on Clinton Street to Canal Street, Kinzie Street to Carroll Street, in the West Division, and the notice's own landmark independently agrees — the committed `north_branch_bridge` lands its west end 'near the south-east corner of Kinzie and Canal Streets', which is one street's width from block 8's north-east corner. That agreement is the finding. What does not follow is the lot: block 8 is held in `blocks_not_in_the_grid`, `generate_plat_lots.py` emits nothing west of the river, and the West Division's blocks carry ten lots and not eight, so 'lot 7' has no cell and cannot be given one here. Nothing seated; the carry to 1835-07-01 refused.

'The School House' of School District No. 1, where the district's officers are elected on 6 January 1834 — a definite article every reader could find and a building this reading cannot. No street, no corner, no neighbour; the committed town holds `watkins_school_house` and `north_side_school_1833` and nothing in this notice says which district either belongs to, so no record may take it on shape.

The dedication of the Presbyterian church, with the order of service and Sproat's hymn printed: 'to Thee these hallowed walls we raise' is a finished building opened for worship. The town holds it as `first_presbyterian_church`, whose `documented_range` starts at the dedication date of 4 January 1834 — this reading's own fact, from the other side. Nothing further is owed.

Lot 3 in block 120 of the school section, offered by Pruyne & Co. in January 1834 and still offered in August. The claim's own note says it: nothing is stated to be BUILT on it. A numbered parcel on the market is a reading about the land market at the town's edge, and it carries no building for a structure record to take.

The Chicago Temperance Society meets in the Presbyterian Meeting House at six in the evening on Thursday 30 January 1834 — a building that can be lit and warmed and hold an audience, one week after its dedication. The town holds it as `first_presbyterian_church`; the use is the same building's, and this register adds nothing to that record.

School District No. 2's citizens meet at the Baptist meeting house on 31 January 1834 to elect trustees. The town holds that building as `temple_building`, whose `aka` reads 'the First Baptist meeting house' and whose function note already carries District No. 2 meeting in it — in the scene year itself, on 11 July 1835. This notice is the same house eighteen months earlier.

The Eagle Hotel, '(Steele's)' — the paper names the house and its keeper in one breath, and uses it three times in one issue as the town's public room. The committed town holds no Eagle Hotel record; `data/structures/` has the Sauganash, the Exchange Coffee House and the Mansion House, and identifying any of them with the Eagle on a shared trade would be a merge no source makes. No street is printed.

'the Building formerly [o]ccupied as the Meet[ing-]House, opposite the bridge over the North [Bran]ch', sold at the Eagle Hotel on 6 February 1834 with the west half of lot 3 in block 44 and lot 7 in block 8 — the same building the December auction cried, re-offered. Both numerals are read and both land in the West Division: block 8 is Clinton to Canal, Kinzie to Carroll; block 44 is Canal Street to West Water Street, Randolph to Washington, on the west bank of the South Branch. Neither is stamped onto a grid cell and neither tier is emitted, so neither lot can be seated. Note also what block 44 carries: LAND, a half lot, and no building at all. Nothing seated; the carry to 1835-07-01 refused.

The Chicago Academy holds a public examination at two in the afternoon on 7 February 1834, so it is a room the town goes into and not a school on paper. No site is given in this notice or in the prospectus of 25 February, and the Academy's ground stays unplaced — the corpus's separate Chicago English and Classical Academy at Water and Franklin is a different school and is not borrowed for it.

Mark Noble Sen.'s trespass notice fixes the steam saw mill by survey: the west half of the south-west quarter of section 4, township 39 north, range 14 east. That is up the North Branch and outside the plat this project models. The reading's value is the one T-0310 could not take off the page — a STEAM mill and not a water mill, and the subscriber's name — and it is kept for that.

'that noted Tavern Stand in Chicago, lately occupied by Mr. H. W. Wattles', taken by an unnamed subscriber who will run it as the Traveller's Home. The building outlasts its keeper and the paper names it by the last man in it, which is the naming habit T-0076 asks the records to keep — but no street, corner or neighbour is printed, and the committed town holds no Traveller's Home record.

The cleanest of the three February impressions of the same trespass notice, and the same survey description: the steam saw mill stands on the west half of the south-west quarter of section 4, T39N R14E, outside the plat. Two witnesses inside one month agreeing letter for letter is the reading's worth; the ground is still off this project's.

The second February printing of the Traveller's Home card, which fixes the surname WATTLES and a middle initial and nothing about the house's position. The house's own name is read from the body copy under display type the segmenter cannot set. No street, no anchor, and no Traveller's Home in the committed town.

The Clerk of the Circuit and County Courts for Cook county removes to 'the building one door West of the house [of] Col. Owen' — an offset, and an offset onto an anchor the committed town does not hold. `data/structures/` carries no Owen house; Col. T. J. V. Owen appears in other records only as a man. So the anchor graph closes on itself exactly as T-1603 described, and one door west of an unseated house is no seat.

The Academy's own prospectus, and what it gives the reconstruction is INTERIOR: two departments under one roof, and charts, maps, globes and other apparatus — a furnished schoolroom in February 1834, now under the public school funds with a board of trustees. It gives no site at all, so no structure can take the furnishing.

The clerk's removal notice running a second week, claimed to record that this impression DISAGREES with the 18 February one: the segmenter sets 'Rast eat ait' where the cleaner setting reads 'one door West'. West and east of one house are two different lots, and neither is a seat while the house itself is unheld. Recorded, contradicted, left standing.

The third printing of the clerk's removal, and the fullest: a house belonging to Col. Owen and a separate building one door west of it holding the county's records, so court house and clerk's office are two buildings. The identification of 'Col. Owen' with the Indian agent Thomas J. V. Owen is deliberately not made by the paper and is not made here; the anchor stays unseated and the office unplaced.

The Infant School House holds a public examination at ten in the morning on 12 March 1834, with patrons, subscribers and a board of trustees under J. T. Temple as secretary. The town holds the building as `chappel_infant_school` — `aka` 'the infant school' — whose function note carries exactly this occupancy, 'Eliza Chappel's infant school occupied this house in 1833-34', and the move into the Presbyterian church during 1834.

School District No. 1's legal voters meet at 'th[ei]r School House' on the last Saturday in March to elect a clerk, an assessor and a collector — a district that owns a building and says so in a possessive rather than an address. The contrast with District No. 2 borrowing a church is the reading's value. No position is given and none is inferred onto either school house the town holds.

John Wright's 'Two Buildings to Let' standing into March 1834, cut at the enquiry line. The same advertisement the town's `wright_building_to_let_a` and `wright_building_to_let_b` are raised from, both citing `chicago_democrat_1833_11_26`. The stock engraving over it stays quarantined as a generic printer's cut, as that issue's source record requires.

The Eagle Hotel in Chicago, named as the house a Cook county political meeting will sit in at two in the afternoon on 12 April 1834 — so it has a room that will take a public meeting and is not a two-room tavern. No position is given, and the committed town holds no Eagle record for the use to land on.

'the court house in the town of Chicago', stated as a fact of procedure: the Cook Circuit Court's May term is to be holden there on 14 May 1834. The town's only court house record, `cook_county_courthouse_1835`, is dated by Andreas to completion in October 1835 and is therefore a LATER building than this one; nothing in the notice says where the 1834 court house stood, so it stands documented and unplaced.

A paid lecture on caloric in the Baptist Church at six on a Monday evening in March, for the Infant School's benefit — so the church is lit and warmed enough for a paying audience after dark at the end of a Chicago winter. The building is the town's `temple_building`, whose `aka` names it the First Baptist meeting house; the use belongs to that record and this register adds nothing to it.

S. W. Reed's cabinet shop sold up, and the inventory describes the interior: three first-rate cabinet benches — the number of workmen it held, agreeing with the two or three journeymen he advertised for — a full set of tools, hardware, and cherry lumber. The sale is AT the shop, so it is a building a crowd can be gathered in. No street is printed and the town holds no Reed shop.

'There is a good Log House and Stable, and about two thousand rails on the ground' — a pre-emption claim thirteen miles from Chicago, which is off this project's ground by the notice's own measure. It is kept because it is the only description in the month of what an ordinary improved Cook county claim consisted of, and no direction from the town is given or inferred.

The March printing of John Wright's two lettable buildings that carries the enquiry line whole: offered since 26 November 1833, still on the market at the end of March 1834, possession immediate, term to 1 June. The pair stands in the committed town as `wright_building_to_let_a` and `wright_building_to_let_b`, raised from this very advertisement.

The levy in Snow v. Saunders fixes the attached dwelling house by survey in township 40 north, range 14 east — a township NORTH of the one the town stands in, so the house is outside the plat, and the claim says so itself. The section number is cut and is not supplied, and '40' is quoted as the transcription gives it rather than corrected to 39 to bring the house into town.

The editor's own sentence on the spring building season opening in the week before 8 April 1834: the mechanic busy at his business, new buildings being erected and arrangements for putting up others. No count survives here — the line that would carry one is debris the transcription flags — and no site is named, so it is a rate and a season and not a building.

'Seven or eight buildings have [b]een rais[ed in] this town within the past week.' A dated count of the fabric going up, and the most useful sentence April 1834 prints for a reconstruction. It says nothing about WHERE, so nothing may be sited from it; it is spent on the town's rate of growth and on no roof.

Two buildings. The first is a dwelling house on lot 3 in block 18, and that seats: block 18 is `blk_south_water_lasalle` (La Salle to Clark, South Water to Lake), lot 3 is the north row second from the west, and the committed cell is `blk_south_water_lasalle#02`, fronting South Water Street — which is what a town-of-Chicago dwelling house on that block's principal face should front. The cell reads `at_capacity` today with four roofs the T-1199 deal put there, none of them from this notice. The second building is a shed or store room 'adjoining and in the rear of J. B. Beaubien's store house', and it reaches nothing: the town stands `jb_beaubien_homestead` and `beaubien_barn` on the Fort Dearborn reservation, which is not platted and has no lot cells, and no Beaubien STORE house is modelled at all. Nothing placed; the carry refused.

'ONE or two Rooms [in this town,] su[it]able for office[s for] Attorne[ys,] [Physi]cians' — a to-let notice whose value is that the building has more than one storey of usable room in the spring of 1834. It names no street and no owner in this half, and the signature that falls in the interleaved column is not part of the quote, so nothing is minted from it.

An infant school with enough children in it to speak at a funeral in April 1834, read off the heading over a set of verses. The claim's own note is the ruling: NO BUILDING IS PLACED — an infant school is a class as often as it is a house, and nothing here says where it met. The institution is the reading and the town is what it is spent on.

'Wanted to rent a Store for the [—] [—]ts.— in a central part of the town.' Two lines, and what they document is that by April 1834 the town HAD a central part an advertiser could ask for without naming a street. A central part is not an address; no building is identified, let alone seated.

A small building suitable for an office or a small family, with panel doors and handsome windows, near Newberry & Dole's — finished joinery at the bottom of the size range, which is the month's best single building description. The anchor IS a building the town holds (`newberry_dole_warehouse`), and 'near' is not an offset a lot can be read off, so the notice reaches no seat on T-1603's ground.

A small building offered for sale on condition it be removed from the premises it stands on — the second such notice in the month, and evidence that a small frame in this town was treated as movable stock. No street is named, so nothing places it, and a building whose whole advertisement is that it can be moved is the last one a reconstruction should seat.

The senior printing of A. Sweet's notice, dated 6 May 1834 and still running eight weeks later: a small building near Messrs. Newberry & Dole's Store, with six-panel doors and window frames offered beside it as stock. The anchor is held and the offset is not printed; the joinery is stock and not part of the building.

G. Spring's For-Sale notice, first printing: 'LOT No. 7, in block No. 16, one lot east of Haddock's Tavern, on Lake street', with a large dwelling house and a fine well on it. THIS IS THE READING THE BLOCK NUMBERING FILE WAS FETCHED FOR and it now seats: block 16 is `blk_south_water_dearborn` (Dearborn to State, South Water to Lake), lot 7 is the south row third from the west, and the committed cell is `blk_south_water_dearborn#05` — whose face is south and whose frontage is LAKE, which is the street the notice names. Three separate readings recorded that this address was the most placeable thing in the corpus; it is now placed. The cell carries one reconstructed H1 house from the policy deal, not this dwelling. Nothing placed from the notice; the carry to 1835-07-01 refused.

'[We offer] for sale the [dwelling] House [on the corner] of Lasalle and Lake [streets] … 16 by 30 feet' — a dimensioned building on a named corner. The town holds it as `lasalle_lake_house`, whose `documented_range` runs from the copy date of 22 April 1834 and whose note quotes this advertisement and names this issue as the printing still running on 18 June 1834. Spent on the structure layer.

Miss Waite's boarding and day school, opening 30 June 1834 'on Ran[dolph-st.,] in a building nearly in rear of the Pres[byterian] Church, between Clark and Dearborn s[treets]'. The anchor is committed and it stands ONE BLOCK WEST of where this notice puts it: `first_presbyterian_church` is on the south-west corner of Lake and Clark, which its own record states as 'the south 25 ft of Lot 1, Block 34' — La Salle to Clark, and the committed cell is `blk_lake_lasalle#06`, plat lot 1. 'Between Clark and Dearborn' is block 35, `blk_lake_clark`, the next block east. So seating the school would mean either moving a documented-corner record on an 1834 notice, which the ladder does not license, or seating a school behind a church that is not there. Recorded as the conflict it is; nothing placed, the carry refused.

A. Sweet's small building, to let, placed only by 'near Messrs. Newberry & Dole's Store'. The anchor is a building the committed town holds and the notice gives no offset from it, so the reading is an anchored building and not a seated one; the doors and window frames on the line below are stock and are left out of the claim.

J. A. Collett's small building for sale, to be removed from the premises it stands on — the plainest statement in the issue that buildings in this town moved. Neither the ground it stood on nor its destination is named, so it places nothing; it is kept for what it says about the building stock's mobility.

Solomon Juneau's lease: 50 feet front and 150 feet rear of lot 1, and 50 by 22 feet of block 18 on South Water Street, the lot fronting on Clark Street. The most dimensioned TOWN claim in the issue and not a building claim at all — it is ground offered for five or six years, and the first frontage figure is bracketed rather than supplied because copying the second onto it would invent a dimension.

The cut witness to Spring's Lake Street notice: lot 7 in block 16, one lot east of a tavern whose name the column edge removed, with a large building and a fine well. The lot and the block are clean, so the seat is the same one the 18 June printing reaches — `blk_south_water_dearborn#05`, south row, fronting Lake — and this setting needs no tavern name to get there, which is worth saying because the name is what the 1834-07-09 setting supplies. Nothing placed; the carry to 1835-07-01 refused.

'122 Building Lots for sale, in the [… ] School section' with two houses to let, enquired for on Lake Street opposite a named man's premises. The number is why the claim exists: a printed count of one tract's unbuilt lots in July 1834. The lines are four advertisements' worth of fragments whose join is not certain, and nothing in them seats a house.

The unexpired lease of the Refectory kept by J. A. Collett, with two rooms adjoining its rear, sold at auction with the entire furniture — a building, its use, its tenant and its plan. The day of the sale is cut away and is not supplied from the calendar, and no street or anchor is printed at all, so the premises stand documented and unplaced.

The printing that names the tavern the 2 July setting cut in half — 'Maddock's Tavern, on Lake street', with lot 7 of block 16 one lot east of it. The lot seats as before at `blk_south_water_dearborn#05`. THE TAVERN IS WHERE THIS SET STOPS BEING TIDY. `mansion_house` carries 'Haddock's Tavern' among its names and stands on `blk_south_water_dearborn#01`, plat lot 5, the south row's WEST end at Dearborn; one lot east of lot 5 is lot 6, and the notice sells lot 7. The structure record already says its position along the block is 'this record's choice' with 'AT LEAST A LOT'S WIDTH' of slack, so the notice is evidence about a placed building's seat rather than about a new one. That is a structure move and a bake, and it is filed as T-1679 rather than taken here. Nothing placed; the carry refused.

The same premises a week later and better described: the Restorator, not the Refectory, with 'two small bu[il]dings adjoining the rear of the same' rather than two rooms, and a complete cooking apparatus among the furniture. So it is a principal building with two outbuildings behind it — a plan, and still no street, corner or neighbour anywhere in either printing.

Three buildings in one notice — a dwelling with its rooms counted, a store on South Water Street, a small building on another street — and the whole of it cut down the left edge, so almost every noun is a supply. A street with no corner, number or neighbour on it is not a seat, and the second street is explicitly carried as an unread guess rather than a reading.

The notice the previous issue could only guess at, printed clear: a dwelling of three rooms and a kitchen on the lower floor, a STORE on South Water Street, and a small building on Randolph Street, all in C. H. Chapman's hand. Three buildings and two streets, and not one corner, number or neighbour among them, so none of the three reaches a seat.

Hiram Pearsons's auction of twenty-five to fifty town lots, some of them WATER lots, 'situate in the most b[usi]ness part of the town'. The count is bracketed because the figure sits in the woven half of the column. Lots on the market, with nothing stated to stand on them: a reading about the land market and the town's business quarter, and not about a building.

Lot 3 in block 41 and lot 3 in block 20, 'on South Water Street, west of the bridge', with a two-storey house eligibly situated for business. Both numerals seat and they are in DIFFERENT TIERS, which the notice's own street phrase only half admits: block 20 is `blk_south_water_franklin` (Franklin to Wells, South Water to Lake) and its lot 3 is `blk_south_water_franklin#02`, north row, fronting South Water — agreeing with the notice, and west of the Dearborn draw-bridge as it says. Block 41 is `blk_randolph_franklin` (Franklin to Wells, Randolph to Washington) and its lot 3 is `blk_randolph_franklin#02`, north row, fronting RANDOLPH, two tiers south of South Water; that lot stands `harmon_log_cabin` today. Which of the two lots the house stood on the notice does not say. Nothing placed; the carry refused.

Lot 5 in block 35 on the corner of Clark and Randolph, and lot 2 in block 18 on South Water Street, both offered to lease. Two numbered lots and a named corner — and no building on either, which is what keeps this a land reading. The corner is supplied from the complementary half of the same advertisement in the 13 August issue and is bracketed, not asserted.

The south half of lots 5 and 6 fronting on Randolph Street, sold by John H. Kinzie for the account of a Dr Fin[ley] whose surname is cut after five letters. What the reading carries is the frontage, that a physician held the ground, and that the town's largest merchant was also its estate agent. No building is claimed to stand on the half-lots.

Lot 3 in block 120 in the school section, Pruyne & Co.'s standing advertisement running unchanged through August. Section 16 of the township sold off lot by lot is a claim about the town's edge, and it carries no building; the line below it belongs to a different advertisement woven into the column and is excluded.

'the houses situated on Lot No. 3, i[n] Block No. 111, now owned by Charles H. Cha[p]man' — a lot, a block, an owner and more than one house, under a mechanic's lien that is itself evidence of recent building. The block number is what settles it and it settles it out: Thompson numbers fifty-eight blocks, and this project's land-sale ground register names 111 as 'block 111 of the school section, section 16 T39N R14E'. Section 16 is south and west of Madison Street, off the Original Town and off this reconstruction's ground, which is also where the Democrat's own 30 April 1834 notice of 'LOT No. 6, in block 111' puts it — 'both on the schoo[l] secti[on]'. Placed, and placed outside Chicago as this project draws it.

The printing that settles the corner the 6 August setting could not: lot 5 in block 35 on the corner of Clark and Randolph, offered to lease by whoever keeps 'this office'. Both halves of the reading are in this claim's own lines, which is why the reading is made here — and the parcel still carries no building.

The one printing of Juneau's advertisement that carries its block number and its second frontage at once: block 18 on South Water Street, 100 feet by 150, with a 50-foot piece off the Clark Street end. A corner parcel offered to lease, with two lots of block 18 on the market in the same month — ground, not fabric.

'A GOOD com[f]ortable D[welling …] contiguous to th[e …]' — and the noun the dwelling is contiguous TO went away with the column. The claim is deliberately weak and is kept for the shape it records: this paper's ordinary way of placing a house in 1834 is by contiguity to something the reader already knows. With the anchor cut, there is nothing to be contiguous to.

The building and its succession are what this claim documents: a store at the east end of South Water Street that Peter Cohen occupied before the incoming firm took it. The firm's own name is cut away in both witnesses and no business record is made from it. 'The east end of South Water street' is a reach along a street and not a seat — no corner, no number, no neighbour the town holds.

A house in Wa-ban-sia to let on reasonable terms, the notice standing all month in three issues and the advertiser's name cut away in every one. Wabansia is a district and not an address, and with no advertiser there is not even a keeper to place it by.

The September printing of Spring's standing notice: lot 7 in block 16, one lot east of Haddock's Tavern on Lake Street, with a large dwelling house and a well. Same seat as the June and July settings, `blk_south_water_dearborn#05`, south row, fronting Lake. What the column can be held to is 'a large … Dwelling House and … well'; the room count and the kind of well are not in it and are not supplied. Nothing placed; the carry to 1835-07-01 refused.

A two-storey building for a store and dwelling 'in South Water Street nearly opposite the draw-bridge', E. A. Rider advertising from next door to the Post Office. TWO ANCHORS THAT DO NOT AGREE, and the reason this cannot be seated. The draw-bridge is the Dearborn Street bridge of 1834, which the town uses as a locator for `chicago_american_office` and `frederick_thomas_shop`, both on `blk_south_water_dearborn`. The post office in September 1834 is not there: Andreas has it leave Hogan's log store for Franklin and South Water about July 1834, four blocks west, and `hogan_store` states that this later office is 'a DIFFERENT, UNMODELLED building' whose construction, size and side of the street nothing reached describes and which 'would be almost entirely invention today'. So the offset anchors on a building the town does not stand. Nothing placed; the carry refused.

An extensive tavern lately occupied by Mr. C. H. Bennett, thoroughly repaired and painted and reopening on the evening of the 19th — and the fuller witness's dateline reads 'Springfidl, Aug. 11, 1834', so the house is most likely Springfield's and no Chicago street or anchor is claimed for it. Recorded with the doubt rather than without it, because C. H. Bennett is a name the Chicago corpus may meet again.

A store occupied by P. S. Carli as a dry goods and fancy store, 'standing on J. S. C. Hogan's lot', to be sold on 15 October 1834. The anchor stands and its lot does not. `hogan_store` is committed at the west end of the South Water / Lake block near Market, on the north side of Lake — that is the Market wedge, `blk_south_water_market`, which `data/reconstruction/1835_lot_ledger.json` carries NO lot cells for at all (the wedge's own arrangement waits on T-0183). So 'Hogan's lot' cannot be resolved to a committed lot even though Hogan's building can be pointed at, and the store on it is a second building the town does not hold. Nothing placed; the carry to 1835-07-01 refused.

The unbroken witness to Rider's notice, and the setting that licenses every bracketed supply in the 10 September printing: the two-storey store-and-dwelling on South Water Street nearly opposite the draw-bridge, the advertiser 'next door to the Post Office'. It is also what places Rider himself. It fails on the same anchor and in the same direction as the 10 September setting — the Dearborn draw-bridge and the Franklin and South Water post office are four blocks apart, and the second of them is not modelled. Nothing placed; the carry refused.

The second witness to the store Peter Cohen gave up, carrying 'have taken the Store' and 'by Peter Cohen' and the copy date of 29 April 1834 — and dropping the 'east end of South Water' the sister printing has. The incoming firm's name is cut in both, so no business record is made, and this witness gives no street at all.

A three-storey store house forty by sixty feet with a sixty-foot wharf front, a two-room dwelling house and a large finished store, all to let by Dr John T. Temple on 20 September 1834 — dimensions being the rarest thing this corpus gives a reconstruction. And the notice does not say the three are one property or adjacent, only that one man lets all three, and 'on South Water-st[reet]' may govern all three or only the last. A street with no corner and an unresolved governing clause is no seat.

Rider's building a third time, and this printing is worth the claim for the ANCHOR and not the building: it puts the Post Office itself on South Water Street nearly opposite the draw-bridge, with the two-storey store-and-dwelling next door. That is a SECOND newspaper reading against Andreas's 'Franklin and South Water', which `hogan_store` already files as an open conflict about the post office's 1834 position — so the notice is evidence about the office rather than about Rider's roof. This register records the second witness and leaves the conflict open where the structure record keeps it; the office stays unmodelled and no lot is reached. Nothing placed; the carry refused.

'A COM[F]ORTABLE and well [f]in[ished] [dw]el[l]ing house [n]ea[r] the point' — the forks of the river used as an address with nothing beside it, which is what a small town's own shorthand looks like. No street and no lot, so the building is anchored and not placed, and the advertiser's surname is single-witness OCR and is not minted.

The October printing of Spring's notice, clean at both figures: lot 7, block 16, one lot east of Haddock's Tavern, a large dwelling-house and a fine well. Fifth and last legible setting of the same address, and the same seat: `blk_south_water_dearborn#05`, south row, fronting Lake. The claim says placing either building is separate work with the plat in front of it; the plat is now in front of it, the lot is seated, and the tavern's own lot is T-1679, the ticket this run files. Nothing placed from the notice; the carry refused.

A store in a two-storey dwelling house 'opposite the Exchange Coffee House', several second-storey rooms to let for offices or a private family, George Smith answering at the Exchange. The anchor is committed and the offset is the problem: `exchange_coffee_house` stands on the north-west corner of Lake and Wells, `blk_south_water_franklin#07`, plat lot 8, fronting south onto Lake. 'Opposite' a corner house reaches two blocks — across Lake into `blk_lake_wells`, or across Wells into `blk_south_water_wells` — and four candidate lots, and the word BEFORE 'opposite' is cut and could be 'formerly' or 'nearly', which changes what is being claimed. A direction is not a lot. Nothing placed; the carry to 1835-07-01 refused.

'the [Bui]lding there[on], formerly occupied as the office of the [D]e[m]ocrat and W.
