`old_bank_building` -- the brick building Hubbard raised and packed in, and here he is telling it himself. AND THE TWO DISAGREE ABOUT WHICH CORNER. The record's own aka reads 'the building Hubbard packed in, Lake and LaSalle'; this page puts it at the corner of La Salle and South Water, one block south. The disagreement is recorded and resolved nowhere: a memoir of 1911 does not move a position the record already carries, and the record is not amended to agree with it. What travels with the building is 'ground that then seemed very far west', which is a measure of the town's extent in 1834 and not of a seat.

`green_tree_tavern`, and the only reading in this set whose own date falls inside the scene year -- 25 May 1835, five weeks before the window closes. `docs/RESEARCH/green_tree_tavern.md` already leans on Hubbard by way of Andreas; this is the passage at first hand. What it carries is a USE, not a position: the house newly landed passengers walked to once their goods were in the warehouse. The record's seat is untouched.

`fort_dearborn_palisade` and `fort_dearborn_blockhouse`, described by a man standing in front of them in 1818. The two corner works and their orientation -- a block house at the south-west, a bastion at the north-west about a hundred feet from the river -- agree with what the town stands. 'A square of about six hundred feet' DOES NOT: it is far larger than the enclosure this project reconstructs, and it is a pace-estimate at sixty years' distance, not a measurement. The disagreement is the finding; the palisade is not resized to honour a recollection.

`fort_dearborn_officers_quarters`, and the fullest elevation of it this corpus holds: two storeys of hewn logs, a piazza along the entire front at second-floor level reached by outside stairs, kitchen, dining and store rooms below, one large room above, under split clapboards about four feet long. It is 1818 fabric and the record is not re-elevated from it. IT ALSO SETS UP THE BOOK'S SHARPEST SELF-CONTRADICTION: this page puts the quarters OUTSIDE the pickets, page 167 (`bk_hub_090`) puts the commanding officers' former quarters in a brick building just within the north stockade and the log quarters inside the pickets on the west. Nine years and a fire lie between the two and this project resolves neither.

`fort_dearborn_barracks` -- the soldiers' quarters, of logs like the officers' except that both storeys were finished and divided into rooms. One sentence, and it is the one that tells this project the barracks were fully partitioned on both floors.

`fort_dearborn_sutlers_store` in the north-east corner and `fort_dearborn_guard_house` -- guardhouses about ten feet square, one on each side of the south gate -- with the two parade gates on the north and south sides. The plan of the enclosure as a man who lived in it remembered it; a corroboration of the corner and the gates, and no change to either record.

`fort_dearborn_store_house` (two storeys, east of the guardhouse and south of the soldiers' quarters) and `fort_dearborn_magazine` (brick, west of the guardhouse and near the block house), with the stockade and every building neatly whitewashed. THE ONE BRICK BUILDING IN THE 1818 FORT IS THE MAGAZINE, and that is why this page matters against `bk_hub_090`, where the brick building at the north stockade is where the Indian agent lived in 1827 -- `fort_dearborn_commandants_quarters`, whose own aka is 'the brick building'. Two brick buildings nine years apart, or one misremembered; the reading records the question and does not answer it.

`fort_dearborn_commandants_quarters`, `fort_dearborn_officers_quarters` and `fort_dearborn_barracks`, and the richest occupancy statement in the book: in 1827 Dr Alexander Wolcott the Indian agent in the brick building just within the north stockade, Russell E. Heacock's family and one other American family in the old log quarters on the west and within the pickets, and voyageur families in the soldiers' quarters on the east side. THE FORT AS A TENEMENT. It is 1827 and not 1835 and it seats nobody in the scene; it contradicts `bk_hub_055` and `bk_hub_058` as set out there; and `heacock_house_monroe` is where this town stands Heacock, which this page does not disturb.

`hogan_store`, whose own aka already reads 'Chicago's first post office' and 'the log store'. This page gives it four of the five fields `data/structures/` wants -- log, story-and-a-half, 45 by 18 feet, and the angle formed by the intersection of Lake and South Water -- and the fifth, the orientation, is implied by the angle and not stated. IT IS A CORROBORATION AND NOT A PLACEMENT, because the record already stands on that ground. The post-office arrangement is described from 2 November 1832 and the same volume has Hogan in the office until 3 March 1837, so the scene date falls inside the span; that is a reason for the structures layer to look at the record's own function note, and it is not a licence for this ledger to write one.

`peck_store`, aka 'Peck's store at South Water and LaSalle' -- and this page is the most detailed description of it the corpus holds: two storeys, frame, black walnut lumber sawn and shipped from Detroit, on the south-east corner of La Salle and South Water, occupied and the goods moved in from the log store in the fall of 1831. Standing on the scene date unless something took it down, which nothing here says. IT DISAGREES WITH PAGE 89 OF THE SAME BOOK about which building was first -- page 89 calls Dole's and Peck's the first frame buildings used for business and dates the pair to 1832 -- and both readings stand. The log store that preceded it is placed no closer than 'close to Fort Dearborn' and reaches no seat. 'What is now' is 1895 street naming applied to 1831 ground.

`mansion_house`, and a USE the record can carry: Cook county's first term of court sat in an unfinished loft of it in 1834. THE BEARING IS THE PART THAT CANNOT BE TAKEN -- 'directly north of the present Tremont House' is a bearing to the 1895 Tremont and the Tremont of 1835 is not that building; T-0385 is open on the 1835 Tremont's own position in Dearborn Street and this sentence does not settle it, so no position is derived here. The compiler's denial that there was ever a brick house in the fort is him arguing with Governor Bross and is recorded as the disagreement it is.

`temple_building`, and a CONSTRUCTION YEAR for it: Dr John T. Temple put it up in 1833. That is an independent corroboration of volume 1's `bk_mose1_012`, which has Caton renting from December 1833, and the two disagree on what he rented -- volume 1 the back room and the attic with desk-room sub-let to Giles Spring, volume 2 a desk in the office and a sleeping room in the attic. Both stand. The Peoria stage line is a business with a timetable and no premises beyond 'the office', which is this same building.

`fort_dearborn_shop` -- 'Fort Dearborn - the shop', function `workshop` -- and a USE for it: Major Fowle set the carpenter shop inside the stockade apart for religious services, and the first sermon by a Presbyterian clergyman in Chicago was preached there by Rev. Jeremiah Porter on 19 May 1833. Whether the shop was still in that use at the scene date this does not say and the answer is probably not: `first_presbyterian_church` stands in this town. The lead surname on the row is `carpenter`, which here is a trade and a building and not a person, and the row's own verdict says so.

`walker_meeting_house`, aka 'Rev. Jesse Walker's log cabin' -- and the first administration of the Lord's supper in a Presbyterian place of worship in Chicago, on Sunday 7 June 1833, was held in it. A USE, dated, for a building this town stands. The cabin gets no position from this sentence and needs none. The three elders are an OFFICE and not building content; Philo Carpenter is a man this project holds, and 'Major Wilcox' is a surname and a rank with no forename, so the project's own John L. Wilcox stays a candidate and not a match.

`sauganash_hotel` -- Mark Beaubien's house, and the town's meeting place as well as its polling place. A USE with a stated day and hour: from 4 September 1833 the Board of Trustees met there on the first Wednesday of each month at seven in the evening. Dated before the window and carried into it by nothing here; the record's seat is untouched and its function already says what the building was.

`cook_county_courthouse_1835`, AND THIS IS THE ONE RULING IN THE SET WHERE THE RECORD DOES REST ON THE READING. The record's `wood_1835` phase carries `documented_range` 1835-10-01 to 1835-12-31, cites `andreas_1884_v1`, and its note quotes this very passage -- 'during the fall of the year (1835,) a one-story and basement brick court-house was erected on the northeast corner of the square, on Clark and Randolph streets' -- as the thing that DATES THE BUILDING OUT OF THE SCENE. So the reading is spent, and what it was spent on was keeping a building off the ground at 1 July 1835. It is not re-spent here and the autumn date is not softened: the court-house is not scene fabric.

`robert_kinzie_store`, aka 'Robert Kinzie's storehouse' -- built at Wolf Point sometime in 1832 and called by Norris the first frame building in Chicago. A construction year and a first for a building this town stands. The second half of the sentence -- 'in 1834 several brick buildings were erected' -- names none of them and reaches no seat; what it is worth is the MATERIAL CLOCK, which is that brick was one year old in the town the scene shows, and that is a fact about the town and not about a roof.

`fort_dearborn_first_1803` on the excluded list: the fort Whistler built burned in 1812 and the town of 1835 stands beside the 1816 rebuild. The reading is kept for the DATE IT DISAGREES ABOUT -- Beckwith's footnote, at eighty years' distance, says 1803, and this project already holds 1804 from Hubbard (`bk_hub_050`). NEITHER IS UPGRADED BY THE OTHER and the disagreement is the finding. Nothing about the fort in the scene follows from either number.

`kinzie_house` on the excluded list -- 'NO SOURCE ATTESTS ITS SURVIVAL' -- and this is the most vivid description of it anywhere in the corpus: a long log cabin with a rude piazza, fronting the river directly opposite Fort Dearborn, from a man who slept in it in 1818. The piazza is confirmed independently at page 169 (`bk_hub_095`) nine years later. NONE OF THAT PUTS IT IN THIS SCENE: the exclusion turns on survival to 1835 and a description of 1818 is not evidence of survival. The exclusion is not reopened from the research side.

`fort_dearborn_first_1803` again -- the 1804 establishment on the south bank -- and the reading's durable half is the two words 'then discharged'. The river mouth of 1804 is not the river mouth of 1835: the channel ran south behind the beach bar until the 1834 cut, which is what this project's terrain and river layers already model, and what `bk_hub_060` and `bk_hub_061` carry. A corroboration of the pre-cut mouth from a source the geometry was not taken from, and no building at all in the scene.

SPENT ON `john_dean_house`'s OWN DOSSIER. `docs/RESEARCH/john_dean_house.md` cites this page twice -- in the 1818 neighbour list at line 62 and in the 1822/1823 occupancy row at line 126 -- and that dossier is the reasoning behind the house's place on the excluded list. What the page adds is the American Fur Company storehouse itself: round logs, a rail fence, on the river edge about four hundred feet east of the Dean house, erected and occupied by the company's agent John Craft and taken by Jean Baptiste Beaubien after Craft's death, which Hurlbut dates 'in December, of I think the year 1823' (`bk_afc_007`). The storehouse has no record in `data/structures/` and no line on the exclusion list, and nothing in this corpus carries it to 1835; whose house Beaubien was in between 1822 and 1823 is the open T-0894 the dossier names, and it is not this ledger's to settle.

CITED IN `data/sidecars/1835/exclusions.json` ITSELF, which is as spent as a reading in this corpus gets. The exclusion for `john_dean_house` turns on this sentence: Hubbard closes his 1818 inventory -- the fort's group, the Factor House, the Fur Company storehouse and its burying-ground, Hardscrabble, Ouilmette's cabin and Kinzie's house -- with the words 'comprised ALL the buildings within the present limits of Cook County', and it is that exhaustiveness which FORCES the identification of Andreas's Dean house with Hubbard's house of hewn logs at `bk_hub_064`, every other building on the list being placed somewhere this one is not. Two more of the seven are excluded for themselves, `kinzie_house` and `ouilmette_cabin`. Seventeen years before the scene, and what it fixes is the floor the town of 1835 was built up from.

CITED IN `docs/RESEARCH/john_dean_house.md` at line 126, in the row that carries Beaubien's whereabouts in 1822/1823 to the open T-0894. Its own content is a placement of 1819 and the only one in Hurlbut's chapter that lands on this project's ground: Beaubien moved up from Milwaukee to oppose Crafts and built his trading houses at the mouth of the Chicago river, 'THEN about the foot of Harrison Street' -- Hurlbut telling his 1881 reader that the mouth had moved, which corroborates the pre-cut channel this project models from sources it was not taken from. It is no evidence for a structure standing in 1835: sixteen years and a rebuilt river separate the two, and `hh_beaubien_jean_baptiste` already places Beaubien at `jb_beaubien_homestead` by the scene date on Andreas.

`fort_dearborn_first_1803` on the excluded list -- Norris's 'Fort Chicago', built 1804 on the site the fort of 1844 stood on, which is the burned first fort and not the 1816 rebuild the scene holds (`n1844_tf_020` dates that one). Norris agrees with Hubbard's 1804 against Beckwith's 1803 (`bk_fer_030`) and the disagreement stays recorded rather than settled by a show of hands. The American Fur Company's trading station 'about the same time', under the protection of the garrison, is a FOUNDING DATE with no position in this sentence: it reaches no seat, and the one description of that post's fabric in the corpus is `bk_hub_065`, ruled above.

`kinzie_house` on the excluded list, and this is the sketch's most usable locator for it: John Kinzie -- father of the John H. Kinzie who was Register of the Land Office in 1844 -- occupied a house on the north side of the river 'a little east of the site of the Lake House', and leaf 22 repeats it. The Lake House is ground this project holds (`lake_house_construction` stands, `lake_house_finished` is excluded), so the bearing is readable. IT IS STILL NOT A SURVIVAL: this is a recollection of August 1812 written in 1844, the exclusion turns on nothing attesting the house in 1835, and a locator is not a date.

A GARRISON STRENGTH AND NO FABRIC: Fort Dearborn as it was understood at Mackinaw before Hubbard ever saw it, 'a frontier post garrisoned by two companies of soldiers'. Two companies is a number this project can hold against the fort's own returns when it reads them, and it is a number about the garrison and not about a building; it names no quarters, no store, no gate and no wall. Filed `kind: building` and carrying none.

THE REGISTER DOES NOT NAME A CHURCH -- not on this page and not on any of the eleven. It heads its entries 'Chicago', 'Chicago Cook Co.' and 'Chicago Ill.' and never a street, a chapel or a house. What the book establishes is a DATE: a Catholic priest was baptising at Chicago from 22 May 1833 and the register he opened that day is headed '1er Page', so the parish's own recordkeeping begins there and not before. `st_marys_church` stands in this town on other evidence entirely, and where the first church stood is NOT read out of these scans and must not be taken from them.

HARDSCRABBLE, AND OUTSIDE THIS SCENE TWICE OVER. John Crafts's trading house stood 'about half a mile below Bridgeport' -- roughly four miles up the South Branch from the town this project models, off the reconstruction's ground entirely -- and it is Crafts's up to 1819, sixteen years before the window. What it is kept for is the CATCHMENT: outfits to Rock River and 'within a range say of a hundred miles of Chicago' is a measured statement of how far the Chicago trade reached, and it is Hubbard's rather than Hurlbut's. Note also the habit: 'Bridgeport' did not exist in 1835, so a house of 1818 is being located by a landmark of 1881. This project should expect that in recollection and never repeat it.

MARK BEAUBIEN'S SMALL FRAME BUILDING 'NEAR MR. NOBLE'S HOUSE', where the first Sunday school in Chicago met from 19 August 1832. THE ANCHOR IS NOT IN THE TOWN, and that is checkable in one grep: `data/structures/` holds no record for a Noble house and `data/exclusions.json` does not name one, so there is no committed coordinate for 'near' to be near. Placing this building would mean inventing the anchor first and then a distance and a bearing from it, which is three inventions wearing one citation. The ruling this replaces said the project holds the Noble house; it does not, and that was the reason to look. THE CONDITION IS THE LOSS HERE AND IT IS WORTH NAMING: on the day the school opened the building 'had neither doors nor windows, and was very imperfectly roofed', which is exactly the kind of material fact the renderer can carry and exactly the kind that cannot be carried thirty-four months forward — a half-finished frame in August 1832 is, by 1 July 1835, finished or moved or gone, and the page does not say which. THE SECOND BUILDING IN THE SAME SENTENCE IS RULED WITH IT. The school 'later assembled at the house of Rufus Brown, within the stockade of the fort'; this town stands `brown_boarding_house`, and it stands in the South Division at local ENU E 428 N -30, outside the palisade rather than within it. Whether Brown's house of 1832 inside the stockade and Brown's boarding house of 1835 outside it are one building moved, two buildings, or one misremembered enclosure is not settled here and is not settled by this page, which never mentions the boarding house; nothing is moved on the strength of a 1832 recollection and the disagreement is recorded rather than resolved. The lead surname `carpenter` reaches Philo Carpenter, who is in the town already and whose presence at a Sunday school in 1832 is not a building.

THE BUILDING AFTERWARDS KNOWN AS TIPPECANOE HALL, 'situated at the southeast corner of Kinzie and State streets', fitted up for Episcopal services at John H. Kinzie's expense. THE CORNER IS THE BEST LOCATOR IN THE WHOLE SET AND IT RESOLVES: `kinzie` and the north-bank Wolcott line — Wolcott Street is today's North State Street, the equivalence `cobweb_castle` is placed on — are both committed in `data/streets/1835.json`, and the southeast quadrant of their crossing is the north-bank tier block `blk_kinzie_dearborn_north`'s eastern neighbour at the foot of State, the ground the Agency House stands on the river side of. So the locator survives and is written down. THE DATE IS WHAT REFUSES IT, and the page refuses itself: the paragraph before is dated 19 October 1834, the word is 'Later', and the sentence after has Kinzie donating two lots at Cass and Illinois for a permanent church building — St. James', which is 1836-37. So the fitting-up falls somewhere in a bracket about two years wide with 1835-07-01 inside it, and nothing in the paragraph narrows it. Splitting that bracket to put a building in the scene would be choosing the answer. THE NAME IS ANACHRONISTIC AND IS NOT A DATE EITHER: the Tippecanoe campaign is 1840, 'afterwards known as' says so, and a name coined five years after the scene tells us nothing about the fabric in 1835 — it is not read as evidence that the building is later, any more than as evidence that it is earlier. WHAT WOULD SETTLE IT is one dated notice of Episcopal service at Kinzie and State in the 1834-35 Chicago Democrat or Chicago American, a corpus this project has read for other purposes; the candidate is recorded so that reading lands on finished work. The lead surname `hall` is the building's name and not a person.

COLONEL OWINGS'S HOUSE, 'about 80 rods to the south' of the Fur Company house Col. Beaubien occupied, 'but since washed away by the Lake'. EIGHTY RODS IS 1,320 FEET, ABOUT 402 m, AND THE PROJECT CAN MEASURE IT THE MOMENT IT HAS A POINT TO MEASURE FROM. It has none. The Fur Company house Beaubien took is this project's `john_dean_house`, and `john_dean_house` IS ON THE EXCLUSION LIST — refused for the 1835 scene because no source attests its survival past 1818 and because nothing dimensions it. So the anchor is a building this project has found in writing not to stand here, and a 402 m bearing off it would place Owings's house on the strength of the absence of the house it is measured from. THE BEARING IS ALSO ONE-DIMENSIONAL: 'about 80 rods to the south' fixes a distance along one axis and says nothing about the across-shore offset, on ground where the across-shore axis is the whole question — the 1815-18 lakefront at the foot of Randolph, the 1828 cut, the 1833-34 piers and an eroding shore are four different waterlines in twenty years. AND THE HOUSE'S OWN FATE POINTS THE WRONG WAY FOR THE SCENE. 'Since washed away by the Lake' is a terminus before 1844 with no beginning: the ground it stood on is gone, so an 1835 placement would have to reconstruct both the building and the shore under it, and Norris is describing 1832. Refused on the anchor and refused on the carry. THE OTHER TWO BUILDINGS IN THE SAME SENTENCE ARE ALREADY THE TOWN'S and are corroborated rather than placed: 'Cobweb Castle, on block No. 1' is `cobweb_castle`, whose own record reaches the same corner from Wau-Bun and Andreas, and the Fur Company house is `john_dean_house` and its exclusion. Norris's block number for Cobweb Castle is worth recording as an independent check on a position this project derived without it.

NORRIS'S INVENTORY OF WHAT STOOD AT CHICAGO IN 1832 BESIDES THE FORT — five buildings, and it is the pre-boom floor the scene was built up from. THREE ARE ALREADY THE TOWN'S OR ALREADY REFUSED: John Kinzie's dwelling east of the Lake House is `kinzie_house`, excluded as gone by the scene date; Mark Beaubien's tavern 'on the site of the Sauganash, generally known as the Eagle' is `sauganash_hotel`; Robinson the Indian chief's cabin at Wolf Point is `robinson_caldwell_cabins`. TWO REACH THE PLAT AND NOTHING HOLDS THEM, and both are worked here and refused. (1) THE LOG BUILDING AT THE CORNER OF DEARBORN AND SOUTH WATER STREETS. Both streets are committed and the crossing resolves, but a corner is four quadrants: the two landward ones are block 16, `blk_south_water_dearborn`, and block 17, `blk_south_water_clark`, both numbered off Wright's sheet, and the two river-side ones are the unplatted margin where this project's own reading of that frontage has already refused building positions at every tolerance. No quadrant is named and no lot is given, so the locator stops at a crossing and reaches two blocks. (2) THE BUILDING ON BLOCK 14, AND THIS PROJECT REFUSES THAT BLOCK BY NAME. `data/traces/thompson_block_numbering.json` reads Wright's numerals off the sheet by cutting each crop from the block's own committed street lines, and its `refused` list names 'blocks 14 and 15, on the Carroll-Fulton band east of the North Branch' — refused because the grid does not reach that ground, so there is no cell on the map to put a building in. A block number the project cannot place is not a placement, and inventing the cell to receive the building would be inventing the plat. THE FORWARD CARRY IS REFUSED FOR BOTH REGARDLESS, and this is the whole weight of the unit: Norris is inventorying 1832, three years before the scene, and under the ladder ratified 2026-09-03 that promotes nothing about 1 July 1835. What the reading fixes is the FLOOR — five buildings in the whole of Chicago — and that is a fact about the town and not a seat for a roof.

THE FORT STANDING IN THE SCENE, dated from outside the window by a span rather than a date. Norris, printing in 1844, has the fort rebuilt in 1816 -- the page's '1617' is an unmistakable OCR slip and the repair is in `normalized` only, per this domain's rule -- named Fort Dearborn, and 'occupied by a garrison, except at short intervals, until 1837, when it was finally evacuated and never re-occupied as a military post'. 1 July 1835 falls inside that span, so Norris corroborates a GARRISONED Fort Dearborn at the scene date, which is what the fort parcel in `data/structures/` already stands. It corroborates and does not promote: no confidence moves, no position moves, and an 1844 sketch does not become an 1835 source by spanning one.

Section 4 of the village ordinances of 7 November 1833 fines two dollars for discharging any firearm inside the corporation from 10 December next. It is one of the most telling sentences in the corpus about what the town was like -- a place where enough men fired guns in the streets that a fine was worth writing down, in the same month as the hog ordinance and the stove-pipe ordinance -- and it names no street, no lot and no building. Nothing is placed.

The June 1834 code puts every street and alley in the corporation, and every road and bridge for one mile out from the centre, under a single Supervisor, with power to abate nuisances and remove obstructions. The one-mile radius is the corporation's own measure of how far its maintenance reached and is worth having; it is not a corridor, and no road is drawn, extended or surfaced to a radius an ordinance states. The plural 'roads and bridges' agrees with the two plank bridges the paper's first number carries, and those bridges take their documentary carry from the ordinances written onto their own records in this pass -- this reading's subject is the officer and the radius, and it adds nothing either bridge record could hold alone.

Three days' labour a year on the streets, bridges and highways within a mile of the centre from every male resident between twenty-one and sixty, or seventy-five cents a day for each day refused. This is WHO made the road surface a visitor walks on and how much of it there was budget for, and it is the most useful thing the June 1834 code says about the streets. It is still a labour rule: it fixes no width, no material, no camber and no extent, and no surface in the reconstruction is changed by it.

The town's revenue machinery, four weeks after the assessment clause: the collector gives a bond of double the tax list, calls personally on every resident charged, and after ten days may seize and sell personal property on five days' notice. A town that legislates this in its first summer is a town with property worth listing, and the ordinance is why a tax list exists for anyone to read. It names no property, no lot and no building, and nothing is placed from it.

The Sunday closing ordinance: no tippling house or grocery in the town of Chicago may sell spirituous, vinous or fermented liquors on the Sabbath, five dollars a breach, in force from 15 September 1834. It dates what the groceries and taverns already on the plat were doing on a Sunday in the autumn before the scene year, which is a real finding about the town; it names not one of them. The clerk is not minted either -- two damaged witnesses disagree and two damaged readings that disagree are not a name.

One fire warden to each of the four wards, appointed by the ordinance of 20 September 1834 -- and only Edward F. Hunter's name survives the column. 'William Wor.' is cut at the edge and the other two are single-witness OCR the claim deliberately leaves unminted. An appointment is an office and not a thing on the ground: no engine, hook, ladder, bucket or warden's house is documented anywhere in this notice, and none is placed.

The ordinance repeals an earlier fire ordinance of 1 November 1833 and takes effect on 5 October 1834, signed by J. H. Kinzie as President of the Board of Trustees. It is what puts the ward division of its own sitting in force for the whole month this pass reads, which is worth recording, and it is pure law: a repeal and a commencement date place nothing. The repealed ordinance's year is bracketed in the claim because its digits are gone, and that reading is not firmed up here.

Three numbers from the August 1835 code that describe a Chicago street better than any picture this project holds: no building material may be left in a street at all without the trustees' leave; a builder may occupy the street beside his own lot but not more than HALF the sidewalk nor half the carriage way, and for no longer than two months; and goods may stand on the sidewalk in front of a store no farther than FOUR FEET into it. That is timber piled against half a footway and boxes four feet out from a shop front, both ordinary enough to legislate about. It is a rule and not a placement: it names no street, no store and no pile, and the street-edge, trade-goods and enclosure layers are not extended, narrowed or dressed on the strength of it.

Nothing dead may be thrown into the Chicago River or left upon its banks; nothing dead may be left lying on a lot or in the alley between a lot and its street; the President and each Trustee may abate a nuisance the moment they hear of one; and a billiard table or faro bank carries twenty-five dollars, the heaviest penalty in the code. Read beside the fire wardens' house-by-house inspection it is a picture of a town of some three thousand that had already worked out it must police what its own back lots held. It is conduct and not fabric: no alley, bank, lot or premises is named, and nothing is placed or cleared.

Section 14 shuts every grocery and tippling house on the Sabbath, in the same breath as the clause letting the trustees pull an obstruction down and charge the delinquent five dollars and the cost of doing it. The useful half is the vocabulary: a 'tippling house' is named as a DIFFERENT kind of premises from a grocery, which is this corpus's only statement that the two were distinct things in 1835 Chicago and bears on what sign a modelled storefront may carry. It names no premises and no sign, so nothing is placed; carrying the distinction into the signage layer is that layer's work.

The single most modellable sentence in the August 1835 code, and it still places nothing. Section 18 requires every stove pipe or chimney passing through a roof to be carried AT LEAST EIGHTEEN INCHES above it, forbids a stove pipe through a side or end wall altogether, and requires a pipe passing a wooden or lath-and-plaster partition to be sleeved in stone or earthenware surrounded by brick, or run through a tin or sheet-iron plate held a quarter inch clear with three inches clear of any woodwork. That is roof geometry, and it is town law: it applies to no named building, and adopting it as an archetype rule would change hundreds of roofs on the authority of an ordinance rather than of any evidence about those roofs. The rule is on the record for the archetype work that would own it; nothing in this pass moves a pipe.

The wards are numbered and the warden of the ward a fire breaks out in becomes warden in chief over the other wardens and over everyone present, in force from 25 October 1834. That makes the boundaries of 20 September operational rather than administrative and gives the town its first chain of command -- a fact about the corporation and not about the ground. No boundary is cut from it, and the clause naming the warden's own number or badge is itself cut mid-sentence at the column edge and left unread rather than completed.

A polygon, walked street by street, and the parent ticket's acceptance asks for it by name. Washington street at the United States Reservation, west to Canal Street, north to Kinzie Street, east to Wolcott street, thence to Illinois Street, thence to Lake Michigan: six vertices, every one of them a street this reconstruction already carries, describing the ground the Trustees thought dense enough that a hay stack in it was a fire risk. It is the only documented statement in the corpus of where the BUILT town was held to end in the scene year, and that is exactly why it must not be drawn -- a density read off a fire rule would be this project inferring the town from its by-laws instead of from its lots. The same section's nine monthly inspections of 'every house, store or shop' in each district are a duty and name no house. The polygon stands on the record as geography the corpus carries.

The postmaster's own timetable, February 1834: Eastern in Wednesday and out Thursday at 8 A.M.; Western, Northern and Southern all in Tuesday, the first two out Thursday at 6 A.M. and the Southern out Saturday at 6 A.M. It is the strongest statement in the corpus of what the post office DID as opposed to who had letters waiting in it -- a crowd on Tuesday and Wednesday and departures before dawn on Thursday -- and there is no post-office record for it to be written onto.

The same four mails a month later, and the reading worth keeping is the rhythm: every one of them arrives Tuesday or Wednesday and leaves Thursday at six, except the Southern which leaves Saturday. So the office stood idle four days and handled the week's whole traffic in about thirty-six hours, which is also why the Democrat published on Tuesdays -- the paper was timed to the mail. The eight-o'clock eastern departure against six for the rest is the only variation and is recorded as printed. It reaches no building this town has built.

The post office's hours and rules as the American printed them on 3 July 1835, two days after the scene date, signed with the full initials 'J. S. C. HOGAN, Postmaster' -- the printing that settles the project's own worked fixture, which had refused to say the South Water Street merchant and the postmaster were one man. That identity belongs to the gazetteer and is not this ruling's. What this ruling answers is where the notice's BUILDING goes, and the answer is nowhere: the office is documented as an office and the town holds no record of it.

A week on, and the new sentence is the human one: people are collecting letters for their friends at the mail opening, and the postmaster now wants written orders so each delivery can be entered accurately. Sunday opening is extended from one hour to an hour and a half. That is a crowd at a counter, which is how a reconstruction should picture the room -- and there is no room on the ground to picture it in. The initials are cut to 'S. C.' in this printing and completed from the 4 July one.

The heading of the standing letter list -- letters remaining in the Post Office at Chicago on the 31st day of July 1835 -- claimed here rather than the six hundred names beneath it, because minting one standing list from each of its printings is what turned 298 names into 638 persons off the 1834 list. The heading documents the office's monthly return; the names belong to the name-level extraction; and neither reaches a building.

Six o'clock in the morning: the office's opening hour, cut out of both earlier printings of this notice and legible here. An office open from six, kept open after hours whenever a mail came in and opening on Sundays too, is the rhythm of a building -- and the building is not in the reconstruction. Between the four printings of this one notice the whole of it is now recovered, and not one of the four gives an address.

The postmaster's signature and his standing instruction that callers say their letters are advertised, under the third printing of the one July list. The six hundred names above it are deliberately not minted from this printing. A signature documents the officer and not a place, and there is no post-office record to carry either.

The same signature under the next printing of the same standing list, kept because the printings differ in what survives and not in what they say. The claim's own note places the office 'on Lake street' from a physician's advertisement in the 12 August issue -- a street, not a seat, and this ruling does not turn one into the other.

The printing where the heading survives whole, and it settles what the list IS: one list, the postmaster's return for the end of July, standing in the forme through all four August numbers -- not four lists, and not the 1 July list a hurried reading of the 5 August column takes it for. That distinction is the reason the name-level extraction was split off. It documents the office's practice and reaches no building.

The last of the four printings of the post-office hours, from the American: open for delivery from six, an hour after a late mail, an hour and a half on Sundays, postage paid when posted and no credit given, and persons calling for their friends' letters asked for written orders. Consistent with the Democrat's printings and, like them, addressless.

Chicago already had the Detroit mail; what this paragraph reports is a second regular route being concluded to St. Louis, which puts the town on a through line instead of at the end of one. It is the earliest statement in the corpus of the reason the place grew, three weeks after the paper's first number. A junction is a fact about routes: nothing of it stands on the reconstruction's ground, and the name it turns on is read and not printed -- the transcription gives 'Dr. J. T. Truez' and the same issue advertises JOHN T. TEMPLE.

Two of the nine advertised Illinois lines reach the town: Ottawa to Chicago by Holderman's Grove, Walker's Grove and Laughton's, once a week, sixty miles, two and a half days, five dollars; and a four-horse post coach for Dixon's Ferry and Galena leaving Chicago EVERY THURSDAY, timed for 'a perfect connection with the Detroit mail'. Thursday is the day the postmaster's own timetable sends three mails out, which is the corroboration worth having. The coaches' Chicago end is given no address and every grove named is outside the plat.

The eastern mail failed to leave Chicago for a week in April 1834 and came back with its own contents -- a specific, dated failure of the one link the town had to the Atlantic, in the season the editor says the spring business needed it. A service failing is not a thing on the ground, and the office it failed at is not a record this town holds. The column is Vision-read and the claim keeps its supplies inside what the surviving text supports.

The town's northern communications put out to contract for the three years from 1 January 1835: Chicago to Green Bay, once a week, on horseback, bids to the Post Office Department by the last day of December. That is the state of the route six months before the scene date and it is a route -- a horse track to Green Bay touches the modelled ground for a few hundred metres of a corridor the plat already carries, and nothing is drawn from it. The dateline's day is bracketed; '10w42' at its end is the insertion count.

The Chicago-Galena direct mail is DOWN in January 1835 and the Galena mail goes round by Peoria, leaving a good part of the section and some of its most flourishing settlements thirty miles from any mail. By the May 1835 stage advertisement in the same paper the route is running again twice a week via Dixon's Ferry, so it was restored inside four months. A route's interruption places nothing.

The eastern mail at the start of 1835: one trip a week, raised to a trip every other day, with the editor expecting a daily mail within the year. Consistent with the Juliet office's notice that its eastern mails came VIA CHICAGO twice a week, which is the town as a through point. A frequency is not a structure.

The Chicago land office will be opened for the entry of lands at private sale on Monday 3 August 1835, at nine o'clock by this witness and at ten by the two other printings of the same notice -- a disagreement the claims record rather than resolve. The office is documented by its hour and by its register and receiver and never by an address, and the reconstruction holds no land-office building. The land sale itself is a public event on ground this project does hold, and it belongs to the ticket that owns that ground.

What the land office would take in payment three weeks before the private sale: the notes of the Bank of Michigan and of the Farmers' and Mechanics' Bank at Detroit, of the New York safety-fund banks, of the Bank of Cleveland and of the Cincinnati banks. It was read as infrastructure because it describes the working of a public office in the town rather than a business, and that is exactly its limit -- it names no counter, room or building.

The second of three printings of the land office notice, reading ten o'clock where the best-set of the three reads nine. It is on the record for the disagreement and not because it settles it; the dateline is taken from the 8 July printing's legible one, the same insertion. Like the others it gives the office an hour and no address.

The third printing, and the second to read ten o'clock against the deposit printing's nine: two against one, with the odd witness the best text of the three, so nothing is settled. What is not in doubt in any of them is that the Chicago land office opened for the private entry of lands on Monday 3 August 1835 under James Whitlock as register and E. D. Taylor as receiver. No building is named in any witness.

The richest piece of material evidence in the eight scene-month issues, and it licenses nothing. Five hundred cords of merchantable wood -- white oak, hickory, white ash and maple, 'and no other', each cord eight feet long, four high and four wide, measured from half the slope of each end -- to be corded by the contractor 'at such place near Fort Dearborn as will be designated by the Act'g Asst. Quartermaster', with twenty tons of prairie hay advertised beside it. The species list is a real statement about what the timber belt round Chicago held, because the army would not refuse everything else unless a contractor could deliver those four hardwoods within hauling distance in one season. The PLACE is the quartermaster's to choose and this corpus does not record his choice, so there is no woodpile and no hay stack anywhere on the reconstruction's ground.

The parent ticket names this unit as its standing example, and it is refused on exactly the ground it was named for: the wood is to be piled 'at such place near Fort Dearborn as will be designated by the Asst. Quartermaster', which names the fort and then hands the siting to an officer. A notice printed on the scene date itself, specifying species and cord dimensions, still cannot put one stick anywhere -- and being printed on 1835-07-01 is precisely where the temptation is. The signature is cut to 'L. T.' here and completed from the right-hand half of the same lines in the next column. The species and dimensions stand as read.

Fort Dearborn is garrisoned five weeks before the scene date and its commanding officer is named by rank and regiment: Major J. Green, 5th Infantry, commanding the post, authorised to call in all United States arms and accoutrements in the hands of citizens of the country. That is a fact the fort's reconstruction wants, and it is a fact about the POST -- the notice names no range, store, guard house or gate, and choosing one would be this project picking a door. The initial reads J here and S in the June reprint, and the claim leaves it as printed.

A year's fresh beef for the garrison 'beginning the 1st day of July, 1835' -- the contract being let in these weeks took effect ON the modelled day, so a beef contractor was delivering to the fort on 1835-07-01. No quantity is stated and none is supplied. Unlike the 1834 printings of the same annual contract, which name the store house and have been written onto that record in this pass, this one gives the commissary, the sureties and a date and nothing to place.

The arms call-in in the American's own first issue, with the signature destroyed: the rank and regiment survive and the name does not, so the claim mints no officer -- an officer a transcription cannot name is not a person the gazetteer may have. It documents the post as commanded and administratively active three weeks before the scene date, and reaches no building. The regiment is read as the 5th from a single damaged character and is bracketed.

The same notice in OCR good enough to name the signatory, Major J. Green of the 5th Infantry commanding at Fort Dearborn, which is why this printing mints him and the first issue's does not. The fort is garrisoned, commanded, and the collection point for arms held across the county. None of that reaches one of its buildings.

A signed correspondent asks the town officers for two works: 'the removal of the coffins projecting from the bank of the Lake, and the enclosure of the burying ground belonging to this town'. Four facts in one sentence -- the town HAS a burying ground, it belongs to the town, it sits ON THE LAKE BANK, and it is unfenced -- and the lake is cutting into it hard enough to expose burials in 1834, which also dates the shoreline's behaviour at that point. The reconstruction holds no burial ground, and this is not the evidence to build one from: the column is the most damaged in its issue and the notice gives no distance, no bound and no corner. The place stands on the record as named.

The notice does not describe the school house; it does something better for dating and worse for placing -- it assumes one. A school district with trustees, voters and a house to meet in is a going institution by May 1834, and the meeting is called there rather than at a tavern, which is where that month's militia election had to be held. But the district NUMBER and the school house's location are both cut away, and the town holds two school records neither of which this notice can be tied to. Nothing is placed and neither record is cited.

The President and Trustees sat at the house of Starr Foot on 1 September 1834 -- a documented use of a named private house as the seat of the town's government, which is the reason this claim exists at all. The reconstruction has no record of Starr Foot's house. Where the same kind of dateline names a house the town HAS built, it has been written onto that record in this pass; here there is nothing to write onto, and a house invented to receive the citation would be the inversion rule 2 of AGENTS.md refuses.

The library the town voted for in November 1834 is collecting books by Christmas and it has an address: donations to be left at the office of Messrs. Jones & King, south water street, entrance first door north of something the column cut away. So the Lyceum's library begins life inside a merchant's counting room -- a use, a street and a door, and no record in either the structure or the business layer for the firm or the room. Nothing is placed; the address stands as read.

A trespass notice with a legal description -- the west half of the south-west quarter of section 4, township 39 north, range 14 east, 'the same on which the [Stoner] Saw Mill stands' -- which is the only claim in this pass that places an industrial building by survey coordinates instead of by a street. Section 4 of T39N R14E lies up the North Branch, north of the plat and off the reconstruction's ground, and the survey description is exactly what carries it out of scope. The mill's name is not read: the print gives 'Stoner Sere Mil', as consistent with 'Steam Saw Mill' as with a proprietor's name, and a steam mill and a water mill are different buildings, so it stays bracketed. Nothing is corrected to bring it inside the plat.

Notice that a petition will be presented to the next session of the legislature to make and lay out a state road from Chicago in Cook county to Venus in Hancock county, on the Mississippi, given on 5 November 1834. Venus is the town renamed Nauvoo in 1840. A road petitioned for is a road that does not exist: nothing of it was laid out at the scene date and no corridor is drawn, extended or reserved from it. The notice is unsigned in the surviving text and no petitioner is minted. It is the road and not the canal; the canal matter of that month is in other columns.

The commissioners of the Chicago and Vincennes Rail Road are called to meet at Danville on Monday 27 July 1835 for the purpose of organizing -- five of them Chicago men: John H. Kinzie, William B. Archer, George W. Dole, Gurdon S. Hubbard and Peter Pruyne. A railroad whose commissioners have not yet organised has no line, no grade and no terminus, the meeting is at Danville, and nothing of it stands anywhere at the scene date. The dateline cannot stand and the claim normalises none: 'July 21, 1635' names a day thirteen days after the issue it is printed in, and the 15 July printing does not settle it either.

A downstate correspondent, reprinted, going 'for the measure to a man' on the work designed to connect the harbour of Chicago with the navigable waters of the Illinois -- and the sentence that matters here is the last: a COMMITTEE OF CITIZENS was 'appointed at a meeting held in Chicago last fall' to procure the means or ascertain on what terms they might be had. That dates a standing town committee to autumn 1833 and gives the harbour project a local body rather than a distant one. It is a body: the passage is a correspondent's and not a minute, so no names are claimed from it, and it meets nowhere this corpus records. The lost closing clause is left unsupplied rather than guessed.

A state senate seat covering La Salle, Putnam and Cook fell vacant on James W. Stephenson's resignation; the Governor issued his writ to the Sheriff of Cook County, and notice was given that the judges of election in every precinct in the county were to open their poll books on the first Monday of August 1835. That is a public event in Chicago on 3 August, five weeks after the scene date, and the county officers it names were in place before it. A writ and a poll are not things on the ground: no polling place is named, the text is the worst in the range, and the claim's normalisation is bracketed throughout.

The State Bank of Illinois is declared open for business by proclamation 'Done at Vandalia, this 7th day of July' 1835, the Governor having had the stockholders' payments counted and their return showing the two hundred and fifty thousand dollars the incorporating act of 12 February 1835 required actually in the vaults. The document is the state's, it is executed at Vandalia, and it names no Chicago building, branch or officer -- the body of it is a 1,973-character weave of two half-columns and is cited rather than quoted for that reason. It reaches nothing inside the reconstruction.

A COURT HOUSE AT CHICAGO IS DOCUMENTED BEFORE THE SCENE DATE AND IT IS NOT THE ONE THIS RECONSTRUCTION HOLDS. A chancery order of the Cook Circuit Court, sealed 8 December 1834, requires the defendant Michael P. Welch to appear at the next term 'to be holden in the Court House at Chicago, on the fourteenth day of May next' -- 14 May 1835, seven weeks BEFORE the modelled day. So the county's own process says a building it called the court house existed and was sitting in the spring of 1835. The only court-house record this project holds is the one-storey brick court-house on the north-east corner of the square, and three independent Andreas passages -- the town-period narrative, the chronological index at November, and R. J. Hamilton removing his office to it 'toward the end of October' -- date that building to the FALL of 1835, which is why compile_scene excludes it from this scene by date. Identifying the room the May term sat in with a building not yet erected would be an identity ruling nothing supports, so the corroboration is NOT written onto that record and the earlier court house has no record at all. The order carries a second and poorer fact about the same office: the Clerk seals it with his PRIVATE seal, 'no seal of office being provided', so Cook county in December 1834 had a court house and no seal. WHERE THE EARLIER ROOM SAT WAS SEARCHED FOR AND IS REFUSED (T-1700, docs/RESEARCH/court_rooms_1834_35.md). The court had no fixed room: Andreas puts the May 1834 term in the unfinished loft of the Mansion House and the fall 1834 term in an unfinished store about twenty feet by forty on Dearborn Street between Lake and Water, then gives the spring 1835 term -- Judge Breese, 25 May to 9 June, not the fourteenth the order names -- no room at all, and neither Caton's Early Bench and Bar (1893), Moses and Kirkland, nor the Chicago American's report of the term on 13 June 1835 names one. Carrying either 1834 room forward would be the same identity ruling this note refuses for the brick building, so neither mansion_house nor any Dearborn Street record is cited.

Hurlbut's 'By the way of Chicago was the thoroughfare to the Illinois, St. Louis and below' is the size argument the American Fur Company reading was opened for, seen from the route's side. It names no work: no ferry, no bridge, no landing, no pier. The portage and the river traffic it bears on are drawn — the water surface, the traced banks and `data/boats/` are all committed — and none of them is drawn ANY DIFFERENTLY for this sentence, because a statement that a place is a way through does not say where a plank was laid. Taken in the aggregate as town character; no record edited.

Duncan's diary at Washington in March 1829, pressing the War Department for engineers to LOCATE the Illinois-and-Lake-Michigan canal and to examine the route to Lake Erie. The earliest step in the canal this volume records, and the canal is why 1835 Chicago was the size it was — but nothing of it is dug, surveyed or drawn on this ground at the scene date, and the reading's own locator cannot even fix the day (the OCR prints '^oth' and the reading declines to read it as either the 10th or the 30th). Taken in the aggregate as the town's reason for existing; no record edited.

Norris's history of the canal from the 1823 survey to the 1829 board, ending in the sentence this project's whole ground rests on: 'Chicago, Ottawa, and other towns on the line were laid out by the board, and sales of lots'. It is an INDEPENDENT statement of the plat's origin — the Original Town of Chicago was the canal commissioners' subdivision — and that is provenance for the survey, not a work standing in the town. Nothing here is a lot line, a block or a corridor this ledger can seat it on; the plat the scene is cut on is already committed and is not re-cut by a directory of 1844. Taken in the aggregate; no record edited.

The 1821 treaty bower: an open bower with seats for the chiefs and headmen, put up on the green along the north bank of the Chicago near the old John Kinzie house, at some distance from the encampments and directly under the guns of the fort. IT IS PLACED BY TWO LANDMARKS THIS PROJECT HOLDS and it is still refused, because what it is placed is a temporary council shelter of fourteen years before the scene and no source reached says a stick of it stood in 1835. The reading itself already says no structure record is minted from it. Its other half — that the north bank was open enough in 1821 to seat several thousand — is a bound on 1821 and is not spent here either; the bank's 1835 state is read off Wright 1834 and the committed structure layer. Nothing drawn, nothing undrawn. Note also the standing constraint: the 1821 council is Indigenous history and this project stages no gathering and draws no figure, so a bower is not a thing this scene would put up even if the date allowed it.

'Fort Wayne, Indiana, was the nearest post-office, and the mail was carried generally by soldiers on foot and was received once a month.' Hubbard's Chicago of 1818-23, and the scene REFUTES it rather than receiving it: `biz_chicago_post_office` holds an office established at Chicago on 31 March 1831, removed to near the corner of Franklin and South Water about July 1834, and taking the mail on the scene date under postmaster John S. C. Hogan. The office this reading names is in another state and the carriage it describes is monthly on a soldier's back; `bk_fer_052`, ruled `asserted` in this same pass, is what the scene date actually gets — a four-horse stage three times a week. Refused as a fact about 1818-23, and the seventeen years between the two readings are the measure the reading's own note draws.

Duncan's written message to the special session of December 1835: every attempt at a loan under the previous session's act had failed, and he recommends a loan on a pledge of the faith of the State. Five months after the scene date. It corroborates what the scene already shows — no canal works on this ground — and it promotes nothing.

The December 1835 session passing the loan law, with the loan made under it described as the efficient means by which the canal was completed. The reading's own `describes_date` is 'December 1835 onward', so it is the turning point that made the canal buildable and it is entirely outside the window this scene draws. Corroborates the absence; promotes nothing.

Hubbard at every session of the legislature urging a canal bill 'until it was effected in the session of 1835-36'. Filed `kind: infrastructure` and its content is a man's whereabouts: it places a named 1835 resident away from the town for part of the winter AFTER the scene date, which is the reading's own reading of itself ('Nothing here is a building; it is a fact about where a man was'). The resident layer holds Hubbard on 1 July 1835 and this does not disturb that — a winter journey in December is not an absence in July. Later than the scene, corroborating only.

STRUCTURE IDS: `south_pier`, `north_pier`. 'To Captain Fowle, however, are we indebted for the first attempt to make a harbor of the Chicago River' — the man behind `bk_hub_068`, dated by Hubbard's own roll of commands to Fowle's tenure of 3 October 1828 to 21 December 1830. The two harbour piers ARE committed and ARE drawn: their line is read off Wright 1834's two red lines with HARBOR lettered between them, and their dating rests on `andreas_1884_v1`. Neither record cites `hubbard_autobiography_1911` — grep them — so this is corroboration of the works' origin and not the page they were written from. Nothing moves: no bearing, no length, no confidence, and the south pier's disputed starting figure stays disputed, because an agreement manufactured between a survey and a recollection is not evidence.

STRUCTURE IDS: `south_pier`, `north_pier`. Congress called to the importance and necessity of a harbour, an appropriation confidently relied on, and General Scott — who explored the country during the Indian war — addressing a letter on it that was laid before Congress. Read at 1832, and the reading's own note says what it is for: 'the harbour appropriation that produced the piers whose construction leaf 23 dates to late 1833 — the works standing, half-built, in the scene.' THE HALF-BUILT WORKS ARE ALREADY THE TOWN'S, under `north_pier` and `south_pier`, and this is the appropriation behind them rather than a measurement of them. `norris_directory_1844` is not cited by either record. Nothing moves.

Andreas on the corporate limits in two steps: the November 1833 extension to the lake east, State west, Ohio north and Jackson south, and the act of 11 February 1834 taking in all land east of State to the lake shore between Chicago Avenue and Twelfth Street, excepting the military reservation from the river south to Madison. THE LIMITS FILE ALREADY CARRIES THIS READING WORD FOR WORD, at `data/reconstruction/1835_corporation_limits.json` § `the_february_1835_extension`, and it is the file that caught Andreas's year: the act is of 11 February 1835. The first half of the summary also disagrees with the corporation's OWN printing, which this project holds at tier 1 and walks its ring on — the ordinance of 7 November 1833 begins at Jackson and JEFFERSON, well west of State, so Andreas's 'State Street on the west' understates the town it describes. The disagreement is recorded there and is not smoothed here. Held in the aggregate at `documented_in_text_only`; no vertex moves and no roof changes its inside/outside answer.

WRITTEN ONTO `data/wells/fort_dearborn_well.json` § `existence`, whose two witnesses are the 1830 Harrison plan and THIS SENTENCE: 'The well was in the outer inclosure and near the south gate.' The record has cited `hubbard_autobiography_1911` for the well's existence and its position since T-0881 without naming the claim, so the citation could not be checked in one grep; `bk_hub_061` is named in the existence note now, beside the sentence it quotes. NOTHING IS PROMOTED: the plate stays preferred over the memory on the distance (the ring is 52.6 m south of the stockade's ink, nearer than 'near the south gate' would put it), the grades are untouched, and no vertex moves. THE READING'S SECOND HALF IS NOT ASSERTED: 'about two hundred feet from the north gate was the river, a stream of clear, pure water, fed from the lake' is Hubbard's 1818 fort and a description of water that 1835 does not give — the harbour was cut through the bar in 1834 and the committed banks are read off Wright 1834, so neither the distance nor the clarity is carried to the scene date.

THE ACT THAT NAMES MADISON, MONROE, ADAMS AND JACKSON, and it is written onto all four corridors in this pull request. Section 2 of the by-laws of 7 November 1833, page 3 column 5 of the Democrat's first issue: the first street south of Washington shall be named Madison, the second Monroe, the third Adams, the fourth Jackson. The four records `madison`, `monroe`, `adams` and `jackson` in data/streets/1835.json now cite chicago_democrat_1833_11_26 and carry a `name_note` quoting the section, and the generator that mints them, tools/generate_school_section_grid.py, states the ordinance as the authority for the 1835 form of the name. AND IT CORRECTED ONE OF THE FOUR: `jackson` shipped name_1835 'Jackson Boulevard' — the modern name carried back onto an 1835 street, printed to a visitor by the street readout — and the ordinance prints 'Jackson-street', so the record now reads Jackson Street with Jackson Boulevard kept as name_2026 and name_changed derived from the pair rather than pinned false. THE ORDINANCE NAMES AND NOTHING ELSE: all four stay `platted, unopened, unworn` with a zero track and `geometry_confidence: inferred` off Wright's sheet, because naming a street is not opening one. The ordinal order is also the corroboration — Madison first south of Washington is the corporation's own numbering and it agrees with the committed north-to-south order of the four records.

THE GRADUATION OF SOUTH WATER STREET, ORDERED BY THE TOWN AND WRITTEN ONTO `south_water`. The Trustees order the Surveyor to graduate the street so that the centre at the north line of each block is the highest point in front of each block, and further so that the water flows into the river at the intersection of each cross street; attested by Th. J. V. Owen as president and Isaac Harmon as clerk, 30 July 1834, page 3 column 3. That is eleven months before the scene date and it is the documented warrant for a class this record had only inferred: `south_water` reads `surface: graded_earth` and its `surface_confidence` moves `inferred` -> `attested` in this pull request, with the ordinance quoted in the record's note and chicago_democrat_1833_1835 added to its sources. IT IS THE ONLY STREET THE ORDINANCE NAMES, so `lake` — the other `graded_earth` record — keeps `surface_confidence: inferred` off the 1891 chronology, and no other record moves. WHAT DOES NOT MOVE ON THIS ONE: `wear_confidence` stays `reconstructed`, because an instruction to the Surveyor says nothing about how rutted the street was by July 1835 and does not even say he had finished; and the crown profile itself is not drawn, so the ribbon South Water paints is still the flat panel every other street paints. The claim asserted is the CLASS the town legislated, which is the claim the record already made.

EIGHTY FEET FOR A STREET, BY ORDINANCE, WHERE A STREET RUNS TO THE RIVER — written onto the corridor width the whole file states. Section 15 of the by-laws passed 4 December 1833 and printed 7 January 1834, page 4 column 2: an owner or occupant whose lot fronts the Chicago River or its branches, where the street runs to the river, may occupy the vacant ground in front of it 'leaving [e]ighty fee[t] for a stree[t]', on paying fifteen dollars a year in advance to the Treasurer. data/streets/1835.json states `corridor_width_m: 24.384` — 80 ft exactly — and until now that figure rested on the 1830 and 1834 plats alone; the file's `_doc` and `sources` now carry the corporation's own statement of it, in the one place on the ground where the width was a live question rather than a drafting convention, because it is the place where an abutter was being let build out toward the water. NOTHING IS WIDENED, NARROWED OR MOVED: the number is unchanged and this is a second, contemporary witness to it. The other two things the reading settles — that the riverfront ground between the lots and the water was occupied by the abutters rather than public open ground, and that the arrangement was a paid annual revocable privilege — belong to the wharf layer and are not claimed here.

WHAT WAS LYING IN THE STREETS, ITEMISED, AND NOT ONE STREET NAMED. Section 9 of the by-laws of 7 November 1833 makes it unlawful from 10 December to encumber 'the streets within the limits of the town' with timber, stone, brick, boxes or barrels, or to leave the carcase of a dead animal in them, at a dollar an offence. The subject is every street inside the corporate boundary section 1 of the same ordinance walks, so no corridor record in data/streets/1835.json receives it. The list itself is the valuable part and it reaches the yard and clutter layers rather than the street layer — the reading's own note says which ticket it bears on — and nothing in this pull request stacks a barrel in a roadway.

NO GALLOPING, ANYWHERE IN TOWN. Section 7 of the same code, printed a week later: from 10 December next, riding or driving a horse, mare, gelding, mule or ass at a gallop or immoderate rate 'through any of the streets of said town' costs two dollars an offence. 'Any of the streets' is the whole layer and names none of it. It is good evidence that the streets were used hard enough to be worth regulating and that the animals listed were the ones in them, and it grades no record: a prohibition is not a wear measurement. Nothing is drawn.

SIX WEEKS BEFORE THE SCENE DATE, AND THE ONE THING IT ASKS FOR IS DRAINAGE. The Democrat's own leader of 20 May 1835 — new buildings and new business whichever way the editor turns his eyes — breaks off to say that the gutters ought to be drained and the sunken spots in the vacant lots all about the buildings of the town filled up. Two things follow and neither reaches a record: that the town's streets HAD gutters in May 1835, which is a fact about the street section and not about any one street, and that the vacant lots held water. No street is named anywhere in the article. It is kept as the contemporary warrant for the reconstructed wear the town already paints and for the standing water the ground layer holds, and it promotes no `wear_confidence`.

THIRTEEN DAYS BEFORE THE SCENE DATE: streets that 'would disgrace a piggery'. The Democrat returns to the subject on 17 June 1835 and is much harder about it — every day the state of the streets and the vacant lots is worse and nothing is done, the lots and the spaces about the buildings abound with holes filled with green putrid water and decaying vegetable matter, the atmosphere is already poisoned, and there are barrels of putrid meat in a building in the most populous quarter of the town. This is the closest thing in the corpus to a description of what a visitor to this scene would have been standing in. IT STILL NAMES NO STREET. 'The most populous quarter' is the one locational phrase and it locates people, not a corridor; the readings' subject is the town's ground as a whole. Aggregate, and named here so a wear-dealing parcel can find it.

G. S. HUBBARD SELLING LOTS, ELEVEN DAYS AFTER THE SCENE DATE, AND DEARBORN STREET IS THE ADDRESS. The notice offers lots 11 and 19 in block 16, lot 4 in block 93, a subdivision of lots 5 and 6 fronting 45 feet on Dearborn street and a second front on another street, and something in block 84, with some of the buildings upon them. The corridor it names is `dearborn`, whose line is already attested from the Thompson plat and which this notice neither traces nor widens. WHAT THE RULING DECLINES TO USE, AND SAYS SO: the second street of the frontage prints as 'R]alph street', which is no Chicago street of 1835 and is recognition-class damage rather than a name — it is left unread rather than guessed at; the block numbers carry bracketed digits; and the lot-and-block locators reach the plat and the lot layer, which is the building-reading tickets' standing job and not a line in this register. Nothing is seated and no building is placed.

J. T. TEMPLE SELLING LOTS ON KINZIE AND MICHIGAN STREETS, MARCH 1834. Four lots 'fronting on Kinzie and Michig[an] streets' to be sold on 10 July next, a third cash and the balance in three and six months, and — in a postscript — eight blocks in the School Section. The two corridors named are `kinzie`, which the committed layer holds with its geometry attested, and the Michigan Street of the North Division, which it holds as `michigan_north`; the notice is a statement about four parcels and adds nothing to either line. THE POSTSCRIPT IS THE INTERESTING HALF AND IT IS STILL NOT A STREET: eight blocks of Section 16 in one hand in March 1834 is a fact about the school-section sale of October 1833 and about who held the ground the four named tiers were ruled across, and it belongs to the land-sale corpus. Nothing is seated here.

THE STREET IS AN 'L' AND THE BLOCK IS A '3', AND THAT IS ALL THAT SURVIVED. 'TO MERCHANTS AND SPEC[ULATORS] — MARK THIS. [T]HE subscriber offers for [s]ale [a] vacant [l]ot on the co[rn]e[r] of L[...] st[r]eet, being lot No. 4 i[n] Block 3[...]' — Chicago American, 27 June 1835, three days before the scene date. The corner is a locator the plat could take directly and the page does not give it: 'L[...] street' in the 1835 town could be Lake or LaSalle, the block number is a first digit only, and the advertiser's name is gone with the terms. REFUSED AS A PLACEMENT, and kept for three things it does say — that a corner lot was on the market in the scene month, that it was pitched at merchants for STORES and as more eligible than any yet offered, and that the seller expected to break it into 'small[ ]ots to suit'. That is evidence about the land market three days before 1 July 1835, and no coordinate is invented from it.

TIMBER LAND ON THE ILLINOIS RIVER AND 160 ACRES IN THE OAK WOODS. The notice offers the south-east quarter of a section in township 33 north, range 8 east of the third meridian, about two-thirds timber, near the contemplated canal; the north fraction of another section in the same township on the Illinois river; and 160 acres in the Oak Woods about seven miles from Chicago. Township 33 north is some thirty-five miles south-west of the town, and seven miles out is far beyond the modelled box in any direction. The canal line the notice leans on is off the ground too. Outside Chicago for this project's purposes, sound as a reading, and nothing is drawn or extended to meet it.

A GOLD WATCH LOST BETWEEN F. MYER'S GROCERY AND THE PUBLIC WORKS, 5 AUGUST 1835. The two endpoints are the whole locator: a named grocery at one end and the harbour works at the river mouth at the other. It tells you the walk was ordinary enough to be made with a watch and a chain on, and that a reader of the American would know both ends without being told where they were — which is itself a fact about how small the town was. IT NAMES NO STREET, and on a platted grid there is more than one way between any two points, so drawing the line of travel would be inventing a route the notice does not give. Both endpoints are named in this ruling so a later pass with the grocery seated and the pier-works yard built can ask the question again with the seats in front of it. Nothing is drawn.

'THE ONLY WELL-DEFINED ROAD BETWEEN CHICAGO AND THE WABASH COUNTRY', for years. Hubbard's own summary of what his trail was, and as a statement about 1835 it is a strong one: the town's principal land connection to the south-east was a single trail and not a road system. The reach it gets to is the town as a whole and the country beyond it; the corridor it would need is a southern approach the committed street layer does not hold anywhere — `state` stops at local N -400 and the four named School Section tiers are unopened and unworn. Limited to that reach, and the missing approach is filed as its own ticket rather than invented here.

HOW THE TRAIL CAME TO EXIST: a direct path from the Iroquois post to Danville in 1822, extended in 1824 south from Danville and north to Chicago, with trading posts forty to fifty miles apart along it, and so marked on the old maps. Eleven years before the scene date, and every mile of it that this ruling can check is outside the modelled box. The posts are forty miles apart at closest, so none of them is in this town. The reading is spent on the town's connection to Danville and on nothing inside the plat; no line enters the ground and none is drawn.

THE STATE ROAD, AND IT IS THE ONE OF THE THREE THAT IS IN FORCE AT THE SCENE DATE. In the winter of 1833-34 the General Assembly ordered a State road located from Vincennes to Chicago with mile-stones placed on it, and from Danville to Chicago the Commissioners adopted Hubbard's trail for most of the way as the most direct route on the most favourable ground. So on 1 July 1835 the southern approach to this town was a located State road, not merely a trail, and it had been for about eighteen months — which is the strongest single statement in this band about the town's land communications. IT REACHES NO CORRIDOR ANYWAY, for the reason the rule states: there is no record of a southern approach in data/streets/1835.json to receive it. That absence is a finding about the street layer rather than about Hubbard, and it is filed as its own ticket. Nothing is drawn, no road is located across the School Section, and no mile-stone is placed.

THE EXAMPLE T-1587's ACCEPTANCE NAMES, AND THE CORPUS ALREADY ANNOTATED IT AS ONE. The publisher's note traces Hubbard's Trail through Cook, Will, Kankakee, Iroquois and Vermilion counties past Blue Island, Homewood, Bloom, Crete, Grant, Momence, Beaverville, Iroquois, Hoopeston and Myersville to Danville, and records that at Crete a portion had been fenced to preserve it. Every anchor in that list is a settlement of the railway era; the note is the editor's, written between 1888 and 1911, and its whole purpose is to tell a reader of 1911 where to go and look. There is no operation that turns it into a line on 1835 ground, because the anchors postdate the ground. REFUSED AS A PLACEMENT and kept for what it is: evidence that the trail was still traceable, and in one place deliberately preserved, three-quarters of a century later. No modern place-name is carried back onto any record.

AN 1812 SPOT FIXED BY AN 1844 MARKET. Norris's sketch has the survivors of 15 August 1812 marched back to the encampment near the fort, 'about the spot where State Street opened to the river and where the market stood' — and both halves of that locator are of 1844. The market is not in this scene; the reach of State Street he means is not either, since the committed `state` record runs from local N -400 only to +20 and does not meet the river. The event is of 1812, twenty-three years before the scene date, so the calendar refuses the placement as firmly as the locator does. REFUSED AS AN 1835 PLACEMENT ON BOTH COUNTS, and nothing about the encampment is placed, drawn or depicted — the standing constraint in AGENTS.md on Indigenous presence at Chicago binds this reading and this ruling takes no step under it. What the reading is kept for is Norris's own sense of the fort's surroundings, which belongs to the fort dossier.

A SCATTERED VILLAGE ON BOTH BRANCHES, AND THE MEANING OF THE RIVER'S NAME. Beckwith, in Fergus's Historical Series No. 27 (1884), records a scattered Potawatomi village on both the north and the south branch of the Chicago before 1833, and gives the stream name as meaning a skunk primarily and a wild onion secondarily. Both halves are town findings and neither is a street: no corner, no reach, no distance and no side of a branch is given, and the word 'scattered' is the reading's own refusal to give one. THIS RULING TAKES NO STEP UNDER THE STANDING CONSTRAINT. AGENTS.md is explicit that Indigenous presence at Chicago is not a research gap to be filled by inference and that the 1835 data layer reconstructs Native and Métis people through one ticket and its writer's stage only; so the finding is kept, named and left where it belongs, and nothing is placed, drawn or depicted here. The etymology is recorded in the order Beckwith prints it — skunk first — and is not adjudicated against the usual printing.
